cases.name: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Company, an American corporation, filed Philippine Patent Application No. 35526 on July 10, 1987 for losartan, a medicine for hypertension and congestive heart failure (sold by its licensee Merck as Cozaar and Hyzaar). Its local resident agent, Atty. Nicanor Mapili, handled the application. An office action was mailed to him on July 19, 1988; he did not respond, and the application was deemed abandoned on September 20, 1988. Nothing more happened until December 2000, when Dupont's new lawyers asked the Intellectual Property Office (IPO) for an office action. Dupont said Atty. Mapili never told it about the abandonment, and that it only learned of his death in 1996. In May 2002 it petitioned to revive the application. The Director of Patents denied the petition as filed out of time, and the IPO Director General affirmed. The Court of Appeals first granted Dupont's petition. But Therapharma, Inc., a local competitor that had registered its own losartan product (Lifezar) with the Bureau of Food and Drugs, was allowed to intervene, and the Court of Appeals then reversed itself and denied the revival. Dupont went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: (1) Could the Court of Appeals allow Therapharma to intervene in the appeal, and was a petition under Rule 45 the proper remedy? (2) Could the abandoned patent application be revived about 13 years after it was abandoned, when it was Dupont's own agent who had failed to act and Dupont waited years to ask for its status? (3) Does a right of priority under the Paris Convention keep an invention out of the public domain? (4) Would reviving the application prejudice the public interest?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition and affirmed the Court of Appeals' Resolution allowing the intervention and its Amended Decision denying revival. (1) Because the Court of Appeals had already decided both the intervention and the merits, a Rule 45 petition was the proper remedy. The IPO's own rules against intervention bind only proceedings inside the agency; in the Court of Appeals the Rules of Court (Rule 19) apply, and Therapharma had a legal interest because Merck had threatened it with legal action. (2) The application could not be revived. The rules allow revival only within four months from abandonment (the Intellectual Property Code even provides three months) and give no exception, so a petition filed 13 years later was out of time even if the delay had been excusable. (3) Even if the period could be extended, Dupont was inexcusably negligent. Its agent's negligence bound it, and a foreign client has a duty to keep itself updated on its local application: it asked for a status update only eight years after filing, and then waited four more years after learning of its agent's death. The period runs from the mailing of the notice, not from actual notice, so Schuartz v. Court of Appeals applies. (4) A right of priority is not a patent. It matters only when two applications conflict, gives no property right without a patent, and does not take an invention out of the public domain. (5) Public interest would also be prejudiced, because a patent on losartan could end the competition that had lowered prices.
cases.keyDoctrine: An abandoned patent application can be revived only within the short period fixed by the rules (four months under the old rules and the implementing rules; three months under Section 133.4 of the Intellectual Property Code), and no exception extends it. Counsel's negligence binds the applicant, and a foreign applicant must itself keep informed about its local application. A right of priority is not a patent: no patent, no protection.

cases.name: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Smith Kline Beckman Corporation, a Pennsylvania corporation licensed to do business in the Philippines, was granted Letters Patent No. 14561 in 1981 for a term of seventeen years. Its claims cover a new compound, methyl 5 propylthio-2-benzimidazole carbamate, and the methods and compositions that use it against gastrointestinal parasites and lungworms in animals. Tryco Pharma Corporation makes and sells Impregon, a veterinary drug whose active ingredient is Albendazole. Smith Kline sued Tryco in the Caloocan Regional Trial Court for patent infringement and unfair competition, claiming that its patent covers Albendazole. The trial court dismissed the complaint, declared the patent void, and awarded Tryco P330,000 actual damages and P100,000 attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals agreed that there was no infringement and no unfair competition (it noted that the United States had issued a separate patent for Albendazole to Smith Kline under its former corporate name, which suggested that Albendazole differs from the patented compound), but it held that the patent itself was valid and deleted the order nullifying and cancelling it. Smith Kline appealed to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: Did Tryco infringe Smith Kline's patent by selling a drug containing Albendazole, either literally or under the doctrine of equivalents? Were the awards of actual damages and attorney's fees to Tryco proper?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the Court of Appeals with modification. (1) Only questions of law may be raised in a petition for review on certiorari, and the Court found nothing wrong with the appellate court's conclusions on infringement. (2) The burden of proving infringement is on the plaintiff. The nine claims of the patent never mention Albendazole; when the language of the claims is clear, the patentee is bound by it, and neither the patentee nor the courts may enlarge it. The absence of the word Albendazole is not decisive by itself, but Smith Kline presented no extrinsic evidence that its patent embraces Albendazole. (3) The doctrine of equivalents was not satisfied. It requires the function-means-and-result test, and the patentee must prove all three parts. Both compounds kill parasites, but identity of result is not enough unless the other compound works in substantially the same way, and Smith Kline showed nothing about how Albendazole works; its witness was not qualified as an expert. (4) A divisional application only means that the patented compound is an invention distinct from the other inventions in the original application, and Albendazole was one of those others. (5) The awards of actual damages (lost profits proved only by testimony of Tryco's officers, without documents) and of attorney's fees (no bad faith or malice shown) were deleted. Tryco received P20,000 in temperate damages instead, because it suffered some pecuniary loss that could not be proved with certainty.
cases.keyDoctrine: The plaintiff in a patent infringement case has the burden of proving infringement. A patentee is bound by the clear language of its claims, and courts cannot enlarge them. Under the doctrine of equivalents, a different substance or device infringes only if it performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, and the patentee must prove all three.

cases.name: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Letters Patent No. UM-2236, issued in 1976 to Magdalena Villaruz, covers a utility model for a hand tractor or power tiller: a floating ("turtle") tiller with a vacuumatic housing float, a harrow, paddy wheels, a protective water covering, a transmission case, an engine foundation, a V-belt drive and an operating handle. SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc. acquired the patent by assignment and published it in 1979, and it made and sold the tillers with the patent imprinted on them. In 1979 its sales at its Molave, Zamboanga del Sur branch fell by more than 50%. It found that Pascual Godines was making and selling similar floating power tillers. SV-Agro told him about the patent and demanded that he stop, and when he did not, it sued him for patent infringement and unfair competition. Godines said that he made tillers only on special order, to his customers' own specifications, and that his tillers were different from SV-Agro's. The trial court held him liable. It made the injunction permanent and awarded P50,000 for damage to SV-Agro's reputation and goodwill, P80,000 for unrealized profits and P8,000 for attorney's fees and expenses. The Court of Appeals affirmed but eliminated the attorney's fees. Godines went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: Was Godines liable for infringement of the patent and for unfair competition? In particular, did he manufacture and sell the tillers himself, and did his tillers infringe the patented utility model, either literally or under the doctrine of equivalents?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition and affirmed the Court of Appeals. (1) Whether Godines manufactured and sold the tillers is a question of fact. In a petition under Rule 45 the Court reviews only errors of law, and the findings of fact of the Court of Appeals are conclusive. The lower courts had good reasons to reject his claim that he built tillers only on his customers' specifications: he admitted making and selling tillers before SV-Agro started selling its own, which showed that he made them on his own design; no job orders were ever presented; and building a tiller from verbal instructions alone would be contrary to usual business practice. (2) There are two tests of infringement: literal infringement and the doctrine of equivalents. In literal infringement the court resorts first to the words of the claim and, if the accused matter clearly falls within the claim, infringement is made out. The trial court inspected the tillers and found them virtually the same in form, configuration, design, appearance and parts, operating on the same principles, so the claims and features of the patented model had been copied. (3) The doctrine of equivalents also answered his argument that his tillers were different. Minor modifications do not take a copy outside the patent, since otherwise an unscrupulous copyist could make unimportant and insubstantial changes. Similarities and differences are judged not by names but by what the elements do, so devices that do the same work in substantially the same way and reach substantially the same result are the same even if they differ in name, form or shape. (4) Godines was therefore liable for infringement under Section 37 of Republic Act No. 165, and the Court upheld the finding of unfair competition, quoting Section 29(a) of Republic Act No. 166.
cases.keyDoctrine: Infringement is tested by literal infringement and by the doctrine of equivalents. A patentee has the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented article, and making, using or selling it without authorization is infringement (Section 37, R.A. No. 165). If two devices do the same work in substantially the same way and accomplish substantially the same result, they are the same even if they differ in name, form or shape, so minor changes do not take a copy outside the patent.

cases.name: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc. owned Philippine Letters Patent No. 21116, issued on July 16, 1987 and, as they themselves alleged, valid until July 16, 2004. Its claims are directed to a method of increasing the effectiveness of a beta-lactam antibiotic by co-administering a compound, which Pfizer said covers the combination of ampicillin sodium and sulbactam sodium (sold by Pfizer as Unasyn). In 2003 Pfizer learned that Phil Pharmawealth, Inc. had bid to supply sulbactam ampicillin to several hospitals. Pfizer filed a complaint for patent infringement against Pharmawealth with the Bureau of Legal Affairs of the Intellectual Property Office (BLA-IPO), which issued a preliminary injunction for ninety days but later refused to extend it. Pfizer went to the Court of Appeals by certiorari. While that case was pending, Pfizer also sued Pharmawealth for infringement and unfair competition in the Regional Trial Court of Makati City, on the basis of a different patent, and asked for the same kind of injunction. In January 2005 the Court of Appeals issued a temporary restraining order against Pharmawealth. It later refused to dismiss the case, even though Pharmawealth pointed out that the patent had expired on July 16, 2004 and that Pfizer was forum shopping. Pharmawealth went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: (1) Can an injunction be issued in a patent infringement action when the patent has already expired? (2) Which tribunal has jurisdiction to review an interlocutory order of the BLA-IPO? (3) Is there forum shopping when a party files two actions based on different patents but asks for the same relief?
cases.ruling: The Court partly granted the petition. It reversed the Court of Appeals' resolutions and dismissed the petition for certiorari as moot and academic, and it dismissed the Makati civil case on the ground of litis pendentia. (1) The exclusive right of a patentee to make, use and sell the patented article exists only during the term of the patent (Section 37, R.A. No. 165; the term was seventeen years from issuance under Section 21). Pfizer itself admitted that its patent expired on July 16, 2004, and an admission in the same case needs no proof unless it was made through palpable mistake. After that date Pfizer had no clear and unmistakable right to protect, so the restraining order was improper and the question of extending the BLA-IPO's injunction had become moot. (2) The Court of Appeals, not the IPO Director General, had jurisdiction. The Director General reviews decisions of the BLA, but what Pfizer challenged was an interlocutory order. The Intellectual Property Code is silent on a remedy against such orders and the IPO's rules say they are not appealable, so the Rules of Court apply suppletorily and a special civil action for certiorari in the Court of Appeals was proper. Filing the infringement complaint first with the BLA-IPO was in keeping with the doctrine of primary jurisdiction, but the question of extending an injunction was purely legal and was for the courts. (3) Pfizer was guilty of forum shopping. A cause of action is the act or omission by which a party violates another's right, and in both complaints the rights violated and the acts violative of them were identical, even though the patents differed; the reliefs asked were substantially the same, so a decision in one case would be res judicata in the other. Because the forum shopping was not willful and deliberate, only the later case was dismissed, without prejudice.
cases.keyDoctrine: A patentee's exclusive right to make, use and sell exists only during the term of the patent, and no injunction can protect a right that has expired. Filing two actions with different patents but the same cause of action and the same objective is forum shopping; if it is not willful, the later case is dismissed without prejudice on the ground of litis pendentia or res judicata, and if it is willful and deliberate, all the cases are dismissed with prejudice.

cases.name: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Zuneca Pharmaceutical, owned by Dr. Venus Arain and later run through Zuneca, Inc., imports generic drugs from Pakistan and sells them under brand names. Since 2004 it has sold carbamazepine, an anti-convulsant, under the brand "ZYNAPS", but it never registered the mark. Natrapharm, Inc. manufactures and sells citicoline, a medicine for stroke, under the brand "ZYNAPSE", which it registered with the Intellectual Property Office (IPO) on September 24, 2007. In November 2007 Natrapharm sued Zuneca in the Regional Trial Court of Quezon City for trademark infringement, injunction and damages. Zuneca answered that it was the first user and that Natrapharm must have known of "ZYNAPS" (the two companies advertised in the same Philippine Pharmaceutical Directory and had exhibited at the same conventions), so that Natrapharm registered its mark in bad faith, and it counterclaimed for cancellation and damages. Both parties admitted that the two marks are confusingly similar. The trial court found Zuneca liable and awarded damages, enjoined it from using "ZYNAPS" and ordered its infringing goods destroyed. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that registration, not prior use, is how a mark is owned. Zuneca went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: (1) How is ownership of a trademark acquired under the Intellectual Property Code: by prior use or by registration? (2) Did Natrapharm, the first-to-file registrant, register "ZYNAPSE" in bad faith? (3) Even if Natrapharm owns "ZYNAPSE", is Zuneca, as a prior user in good faith, liable for trademark infringement?
cases.ruling: The Court partly granted the petition. (1) Under Section 122 of the Intellectual Property Code, rights in a mark are acquired through registration. The language of the Code, the removal from Section 123.1(d) of the phrase "previously used in the Philippines by another and not abandoned", and Senator Roco's sponsorship speech all show that the old rule that ownership comes from use (under the Trademark Law, as amended) was abandoned. The use-based rule applied in Berris and E.Y. Industrial Sales belongs to marks used or registered under the old law, and the statement in Berris that ownership is acquired by registration and actual use was rectified. So Natrapharm, the first-to-file registrant in good faith, owns "ZYNAPSE". (2) Bad faith means knowledge by the applicant of prior creation, use or registration of an identical or similar mark by another; a registration obtained in bad faith is void. Good faith is presumed, and Zuneca had to prove bad faith. It showed only a possibility that someone at Natrapharm might have known of "ZYNAPS", while Natrapharm explained how it coined its name and showed that it checked the IMS-PPI, BFAD and IPO databases. So the registration stands and Zuneca's counterclaims were rightly dismissed. (3) However, Section 159.1 provides that a registered mark has no effect against a person who in good faith, before the filing or priority date, was using the mark. This lets the prior user in good faith keep using its mark even after the other's registration (it may transfer the mark only together with its business), and the lower courts' reading, which limited the exemption to acts before registration, would make the provision useless. Zuneca is therefore not liable for infringement, and the damages, injunction and destruction of goods were set aside. (4) Because confusingly similar names for medicines can endanger patients, the Court ordered both companies to state on their packaging, in plain language, the conditions their drugs treat and a warning of what each drug is not for, and it directed the Food and Drug Administration to monitor compliance.
cases.keyDoctrine: Under the Intellectual Property Code, ownership of a mark is acquired through registration (first-to-file), not through use. A registration obtained in bad faith, meaning with knowledge of another's prior creation, use or registration, is void, but good faith is presumed. A prior user in good faith is protected by Section 159.1: the registered mark has no effect against it, so it may keep using its mark, and no damages, injunction or destruction of goods can be ordered against it for infringement.

cases.name: Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: On October 21, 2006, Dermaline, Inc. applied to the Intellectual Property Office (IPO) to register the mark "DERMALINE DERMALINE, INC." for skin treatment services under Class 44. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc. opposed. It owned "DERMALIN", registered in 1986 for pharmaceutical products (Class 5), renewed in 2006, and in commercial use since 1977. Myra argued that the dominant feature of Dermaline's mark was practically identical with its own: the first eight letters were the same, both had three syllables identical in sound, and the added letter "E" was silent. Dermaline had also earlier applied for "DERMALINE" and been refused. Dermaline replied that the marks looked entirely different when each was taken as a whole, and that its beauty and health services were unrelated to Myra's medicines for skin disorders. The IPO Bureau of Legal Affairs sustained the opposition and rejected the application under Section 123.1(d) of the Intellectual Property Code. Dermaline appealed to the IPO Director General, but the appeal was dismissed for being filed out of time. The Court of Appeals affirmed, and Dermaline went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: Did the Court of Appeals err in upholding the IPO's rejection of Dermaline's application, that is, was "DERMALINE DERMALINE, INC." confusingly similar to the registered mark "DERMALIN"?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition and affirmed the rejection. A registered trademark owner has the right under Section 147 to prevent others from using an identical or similar mark where the use would likely cause confusion. In deciding whether there is likelihood of confusion, two tests have developed: the Dominancy Test, which looks at the similarity of the prevalent features of the marks, and the Holistic Test, which considers the marks in their entirety, including labels and packaging. The IPO applied the Dominancy Test, which is written into Section 155.1, and the Court agreed with its findings. The marks are spelled almost the same and pronounced practically the same way in three syllables, with the final "E" silent, so an ordinary buyer who hears a radio advertisement of "Dermaline" would likely associate it with "DERMALIN", even though the marks are presented differently. Dermaline's argument that its services belong to another classification does not remove the possibility of mistake, especially since both classes concern skin treatments. The registered owner is protected in areas that are the normal potential expansion of its business, so the public could think that Myra had expanded from skin medicines to health and beauty services through Dermaline. An application for a mark nearly the same as an already registered one should be rejected even without opposition. The IPO's findings on this factual issue, upheld by the Court of Appeals, are given great weight, and the IPO decision had in any case become final when Dermaline failed to appeal on time.
cases.keyDoctrine: Likelihood of confusion between marks is tested by the Dominancy Test (the prevalent features, and the aural and visual impressions on the ordinary purchaser) and the Holistic Test (the entirety of the marks). A different classification of goods or services does not remove the likelihood of confusion, and the registered owner is protected in the normal potential expansion of its business.

cases.name: Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College (Harvard University)
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: In 2005 Fredco Manufacturing Corporation, a Philippine company, petitioned the Bureau of Legal Affairs of the Intellectual Property Office (IPO) to cancel Registration No. 56561, issued in 1993 to Harvard University for the "Harvard Veritas Shield Symbol" for goods in several classes, including Class 25 (clothing). Fredco said that its predecessor, New York Garments, had first used "Harvard" for clothing in the Philippines in 1982 and had registered it in 1988. That registration had been cancelled in 1998 because the required affidavit of use was not filed on the fifth anniversary. Harvard University answered that it owned the name and mark "Harvard" worldwide: the name was adopted in 1639, used in commerce since 1872, and registered in at least 50 countries, and it had never licensed anyone in the Philippines. It had found Fredco's website advertising "Harvard Jeans USA", with a logo reading "Established 1936" and "Cambridge, Massachusetts", and it had filed an infringement and unfair competition complaint against Fredco. The Bureau of Legal Affairs cancelled Harvard's registration for Class 25 goods. The IPO Director General reversed this, and the Court of Appeals affirmed the Director General. Fredco went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: Did the Court of Appeals commit a reversible error in affirming the IPO Director General, that is, may Harvard University's registration of the mark "Harvard" for Class 25 goods stand against Fredco, which claimed prior use of "Harvard" in the Philippines?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition and affirmed the Court of Appeals. (1) Actual prior use in the Philippines was not required of Harvard University: its registration was based on home registration, which Section 37 of R.A. No. 166 allows, and under Section 239.2 of R.A. No. 8293 marks registered under the old law are deemed granted under the new one, which does not require actual prior use here, so any such defect was cured. Fredco's own registration had been cancelled in 1998 for failure to file the affidavit of use, so Fredco was no longer the registrant or presumptive owner. (2) There were two compelling reasons why the petition failed. First, Fredco's use of "Harvard" together with "Cambridge, Massachusetts", "Established 1936" and "USA" on its logo falsely suggested a connection with Harvard University. Section 4(a) of R.A. No. 166 prohibits registering a mark that falsely suggests a connection with persons or institutions, and under Section 17(c) such a violation is a ground for cancellation. Second, the Philippines and the United States are both parties to the Paris Convention. Under Article 8 and Section 37 of R.A. No. 166, a trade name of a national of a Paris Convention country is protected without the obligation of filing or registration, and under Article 6bis, as implemented by the Ministry of Trade directives and Section 123.1(e) of R.A. No. 8293, an internationally well-known mark is protected whether or not it is registered or used in the Philippines. "Harvard" is a well-known name and mark internationally, including in the Philippines, so it was protected even before Harvard University applied to register it here.
cases.keyDoctrine: An internationally well-known mark is protected in the Philippines under Article 6bis of the Paris Convention and Section 123.1(e) of the Intellectual Property Code even if it is neither registered nor used here; this is the exception to the territoriality principle. The trade name of a national of a Paris Convention country is protected without filing or registration (Article 8). A mark that falsely suggests a connection with a person or institution cannot be registered (Section 4(a), R.A. No. 166).

cases.name: Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc. (Phil.)
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Kensonic, Inc. introduced SAKURA products in the Philippines in October 1994 and used the mark for Class 9 audio-video goods (amplifiers, speakers, car stereos, televisions, DVD players and similar items). In an earlier case, Kensonic opposed Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc.'s 1999 application to register SAKURA for similar Class 9 goods and won, and that decision became final. On June 6, 2002, Uni-Line applied to register SAKURA for goods in three classes: Class 7 (washing machines, vacuum cleaners, blenders and similar items), Class 9 (television sets, stereo components, DVD/VCD players, voltage regulators, portable generators, switch breakers and fuses) and Class 11 (refrigerators, air conditioners, rice cookers and similar appliances). There was no opposition, and a certificate of registration took effect on March 18, 2006. In September 2006, Kensonic petitioned to cancel it. The Bureau of Legal Affairs cancelled the whole registration. On appeal, the IPO Director General cancelled only the Class 9 goods and kept the Class 7 and Class 11 goods. The Court of Appeals first allowed the registration of voltage regulators, portable generators, switch breakers and fuses (cancelling the television sets, stereo components and DVD/VCD players), but on Kensonic's motion for partial reconsideration it restored the Director General's ruling that all Class 9 goods were cancelled. Both parties appealed to the Supreme Court. Uni-Line argued that SAKURA is a generic word (Japanese for cherry blossom) that no one can appropriate, and that its voltage regulators and similar goods were unrelated to Kensonic's audio-video products. Kensonic argued that Uni-Line's Class 7 and Class 11 goods were also related to its goods.
cases.issue: (1) Is the SAKURA mark capable of appropriation? (2) Are Uni-Line's goods under Class 7 and Class 11 related to Kensonic's goods under Class 9? (3) Are Uni-Line's Class 9 goods (voltage regulators, portable generators, switch breakers and fuses) related to Kensonic's Class 9 goods?
cases.ruling: The Court dismissed Kensonic's appeal and partly granted Uni-Line's. (1) The SAKURA mark can be appropriated. A mark is a sign that distinguishes goods or services, while a copyright is a right over literary or artistic works, and this case concerns a mark. Section 123 prohibits registering a mark that consists exclusively of signs generic for the goods it identifies, so what is prohibited is a generic mark that identifies the goods. SAKURA, the Japanese flowering cherry, is generic in nature but does not identify DVD or VCD players and the like, unlike "pale pilsen" for beer in Asia Brewery. Kensonic's prior use since 1994 made it the owner, and that factual finding cannot be reviewed in a petition under Rule 45, which is limited to questions of law. (2) Uni-Line's Class 7 and Class 11 goods are home appliances that are not related to Kensonic's goods. The prohibition in Section 123 extends to goods related to the registered goods, not to goods that the registrant may produce in the future, since a right to a trademark should not depend on mere possibilities. Applying the Mighty Corporation factors (such as class, descriptive attributes, purposes and conditions of sale), the goods are unrelated. (3) Goods are not related merely because they belong to the same class. Following Taiwan Kolin, the Court noted that Class 9 can be sub-classified, that Kensonic's goods are audiovisual equipment while Uni-Line's voltage regulators, portable generators, switch breakers and fuses are devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity, and that Kensonic's goods are final products while Uni-Line's are spare parts. These goods are unrelated, so Uni-Line may register SAKURA for them.
cases.keyDoctrine: A generic word may be appropriated as a mark when it does not identify the goods it covers. The prohibition on registering a confusingly similar mark extends to related goods, not to goods the registrant may produce in the future. Goods are not related merely because they belong to the same class; relatedness is decided by the Mighty Corporation factors.

cases.name: Mighty Corporation and La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. v. E. & J. Gallo Winery and The Andresons Group, Inc.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: E. & J. Gallo Winery, a California company, registered the trademark GALLO for wines in the Philippines on November 16, 1971. According to its own admission, it first sold GALLO wines here only in 1974, within the former U.S. military facilities, and outside them only in 1979. The Andresons Group, Inc. has been its exclusive importer and distributor in the Philippines since 1991. Meanwhile, Tobacco Industries of the Philippines, and later La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. and Mighty Corporation, had been using GALLO as a cigarette brand since 1973, with the Bureau of Internal Revenue's approval of the brand. La Campana applied to register the GALLO cigarette mark in 1985 and got a copyright registration for its cigarette labels. In 1992 an Andresons employee saw GALLO cigarettes displayed in a Davao supermarket, and in March 1993 Gallo Winery and Andresons sued Mighty and La Campana in the Makati Regional Trial Court for trademark infringement, tradename infringement and unfair competition. Mighty's cigarette label carries a large rooster device (gallo is the Spanish word for rooster) and the words "MADE BY MIGHTY CORPORATION", sold cheaply through sari-sari stores and vendors. Gallo Winery's wines are high-priced imported products sold in hotels, bars and high-end stores. The trial court, after trial, held Mighty and La Campana liable under the Trademark Law, the Intellectual Property Code, Article 6bis of the Paris Convention and the TRIPS Agreement and awarded damages, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Mighty and La Campana petitioned the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: (1) Which law governs: the Trademark Law and the Paris Convention, or the Intellectual Property Code that took effect after the complaint was filed? (2) Are GALLO wines and GALLO cigarettes identical, similar or related goods, so that the use of GALLO on cigarettes is likely to cause confusion? (3) Are Mighty and La Campana liable for trademark infringement, unfair competition and damages?
cases.ruling: The Court granted the petition, set aside the decisions of the trial court and the Court of Appeals, and dismissed the complaint. It reviewed the facts because they were intertwined with questions of law and the lower courts had veered from the law and jurisprudence. (1) The Intellectual Property Code, which took effect on January 1, 1998, was wrongly applied retroactively to a complaint filed in 1993; the Trademark Law and the Paris Convention govern, and where they conflict, the municipal Trademark Law prevails. (2) Under the Trademark Law, infringement requires a mark actually used in commerce in the Philippines and registered; actual commercial use is essential. Gallo Winery's wine was first sold here in 1974 and 1979, after Tobacco Industries began using GALLO for cigarettes in 1973, so Gallo Winery never enjoyed an exclusive right against the cigarette makers. Its registration also covered wines only (Section 20). (3) There is no likelihood of confusion. The dominant feature of the cigarette mark is the rooster device and the label names the manufacturer, while the wine labels are different. Wines and cigarettes are not identical, similar, competing or related goods. The lower courts' reasons (both are forms of vice, and both are sold in the same supermarket section) were arbitrary, and the products differ in descriptive properties, price, buyers and channels of trade. Tobacco and alcohol are related only in special circumstances, namely when a famous mark is involved and there is a demonstrated intent to capitalize on it. (4) GALLO wine is not a well-known mark under the Paris Convention in this case because wines and cigarettes are not identical or similar goods. (5) Gallo Winery's delay of almost twenty years, with implied consent and acquiescence, and the absence of bad faith, tipped equity in favor of Mighty. There was no attempt to pass off, so there was no unfair competition.
cases.keyDoctrine: Goods are "related" only if the public may be deceived into believing that they come from the same maker, and no single factor decides this; classification, price, properties, purposes, buyers and channels of trade are all weighed. Under the old Trademark Law, the registrant's exclusive right was limited to the goods in its certificate and required actual use in the Philippines. Trademark infringement requires prior registration and no fraudulent intent, while unfair competition requires fraudulent intent (passing off) but not registration. A law is not applied retroactively.

cases.name: Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: In 1996 Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. applied to the Intellectual Property Office (IPO) to register "KOLIN" for a group of goods, including colored televisions, refrigerators, air conditioners, electric fans and water dispensers. After the application was considered abandoned for failure to elect one class, it was revived in 2002, with Taiwan Kolin electing Class 9 of the Nice Classification for goods such as television sets, cassette recorders, VCD amplifiers, camcorders and other audio/video electronic equipment. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc. opposed in 2006. It had registered its own "KOLIN" mark on November 23, 2003, for Class 9 goods: automatic voltage regulator, converter, recharger, stereo booster, AC-DC regulated power supply, step-down transformer and PA amplified AC-DC. In an earlier dispute between the two, the IPO had not given priority to Taiwan Kolin's 1988 Taiwan registration, because there was no proof that it used the mark in the Philippines. The IPO Bureau of Legal Affairs sustained the opposition and rejected Taiwan Kolin's application, because the marks were identical and the goods were in the same class, and it noted evidence of actual confusion. The IPO Director General reversed and gave due course to the application, restricted to "television and DVD player". The Court of Appeals reinstated the Bureau's decision, on the ground that the marks were confusingly similar, that televisions could be considered within the normal expansion of Kolin Electronics' business, and that the goods were used together. Taiwan Kolin went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: Is Taiwan Kolin entitled to register "KOLIN" for its television sets and DVD players, that is, are its goods related to the goods covered by Kolin Electronics' earlier registration of the identical mark, so that confusion is likely?
cases.ruling: The Court granted the petition, reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the Director General's decision. (1) Identical marks may be registered for products in the same class. Uniformity in categorization under the Nice Classification does not by itself bar registration of an identical mark; emphasis should be on the similarity of the products and not on an arbitrary classification, and the fact that one person has used a mark on his goods does not, without more, prevent others from using it on unrelated articles of a different kind. (2) Applying the Mighty Corporation factors, the goods are unrelated. Classification is only one of many considerations. Class 9 can be sub-classified into five groups: Taiwan Kolin's televisions and DVD players are audiovisual equipment, while Kolin Electronics' regulators, converters and similar goods are devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity. Taiwan Kolin's goods are home appliances with a distinct function and purpose, sold wholesale to accredited dealers, while Kolin Electronics' goods are sold in electrical and hardware stores. The Court rejected the idea that all electronic products, or all devices that are plugged into sockets, are necessarily related. (3) The ordinarily intelligent buyer is not likely to be confused. The goods are relatively expensive and rarely replaced, so the buyer is more cautious and discriminating, and the two marks, though both read "KOLIN", differ visually and aurally (italic black lettering against white lettering on a red background). (4) The usual respect for the factual findings of lower courts does not apply where they overlooked, misapprehended or misapplied a fact or circumstance of weight; here the nature of the products materially affects the outcome.
cases.keyDoctrine: Registration of an identical mark is not barred merely because both sets of goods fall in the same class of the Nice Classification. Whether goods are related is decided by the Mighty Corporation factors, with classification only one of them, and the test of likely confusion looks at the ordinarily intelligent buyer, who is more careful when buying relatively expensive goods.

cases.name: San Miguel Pure Foods Company, Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: San Miguel Pure Foods Company, Inc. (SMPFCI) sells ham under the registered mark "PUREFOODS FIESTA HAM" (its FIESTA ham was introduced in 1980). Foodsphere, Inc. sells ham under the "CDO" brand and introduced its "PISTA" ham in 2006. In 2009 Foodsphere changed its packaging from a paper box to a paper ham bag. SMPFCI's paper ham bag is predominantly red and carries a partly sliced ham served on a plate with fruits on the front and other ham varieties at the back, and Foodsphere's bag has the same colors and the same layout. In November 2010 SMPFCI filed a complaint for trademark infringement and unfair competition against Foodsphere in the Bureau of Legal Affairs of the Intellectual Property Office (IPO). The Bureau dismissed it. The IPO Director General affirmed that there was no trademark infringement, since the marks look and sound different and PISTA was itself registered, but found Foodsphere guilty of unfair competition and awarded nominal damages of P100,000 and attorney's fees of P300,000. The Court of Appeals affirmed the finding of unfair competition and said that exemplary damages were also warranted, but its dispositive portion only affirmed the Director General's decision; it later deleted the exemplary damages on the ground that SMPFCI had never prayed for them. SMPFCI appealed on the exemplary damages (G.R. No. 217781), and Foodsphere appealed the finding of unfair competition (G.R. No. 217788).
cases.issue: (1) Did the Court of Appeals err in deleting the award of exemplary damages from the body of its decision, when the body said that exemplary damages were warranted but the dispositive portion did not award them? (2) Is Foodsphere guilty of unfair competition?
cases.ruling: The Court denied both petitions and affirmed the Court of Appeals. (1) On exemplary damages (G.R. No. 217781): when the dispositive portion (fallo) conflicts with the body of a decision, the fallo prevails, because it is the final order and the body is merely a statement ordering nothing. The exception, when the body so clearly shows a mistake in the dispositive portion, did not apply, because the mistake was in the body: the Court of Appeals only meant to adopt the Director General's award, which had been nominal damages and attorney's fees. In any event, SMPFCI did not prove its right to exemplary damages. They require that the claimant first establish its right to moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages, and SMPFCI failed to prove its claimed foregone income. (2) On unfair competition (G.R. No. 217788): under Section 168 of the Intellectual Property Code, unfair competition is passing off one's goods as those of another, and the essential elements are (a) confusing similarity in the general appearance of the goods and (b) intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor. The two packages used paper ham bags, both predominantly red, with the same layout, so Foodsphere's packaging in its entirety (not merely the PISTA mark) was confusingly similar. Foodsphere's intent to deceive was shown by its switch from its old box to the same kind of bag with the same layout, and it can be inferred from the similarity of the appearance of the goods. Unfair competition is a question of fact, and the Director General's findings, supported by substantial evidence and affirmed by the Court of Appeals, are respected.
cases.keyDoctrine: Unfair competition is passing off one's goods as those of another, and its elements are confusing similarity in the general appearance of the goods and intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor; the confusing similarity may come from packaging and not only from the marks, and the intent may be inferred from the similarity of the appearance of the goods. When the fallo and the body of a decision conflict, the fallo prevails. Exemplary damages need an established right to moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages.

cases.name: Joaquin, Jr. and BJ Productions, Inc. v. Drilon, et al.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: BJ Productions, Inc. (BJPI) held Certificate of Copyright No. M922, dated January 28, 1971, for Rhoda and Me, a dating game show aired from 1970 to 1977. In 1973 it filed with the National Library an addendum describing the show's format and style of presentation. In July 1991 Francisco Joaquin, Jr., BJPI's president, saw an episode of It's a Date, produced by IXL Productions, Inc. and aired on RPN Channel 9. He demanded in two letters that IXL stop airing it. IXL's president, Gabriel Zosa, apologized and asked for a meeting, but IXL kept airing the show, and it registered its own copyright for the first episode of It's a Date in August 1991. BJPI filed a complaint, and an information for violation of P.D. No. 49 (the copyright law then in force) was filed in the Regional Trial Court against Zosa and certain RPN officers. Zosa asked the Department of Justice to review the prosecutor's finding of probable cause. On August 12, 1992, Secretary of Justice Franklin Drilon reversed the prosecutor and directed him to move for the dismissal of the case, ruling that the format of a dating game show is not copyrightable and that BJPI had not presented the master tape. BJPI's motion for reconsideration was denied, and Joaquin and BJPI went to the Supreme Court by petition for certiorari. They argued that the Secretary of Justice gravely abused his discretion by relying on the non-presentation of the master tape, which the respondents had not raised, and by deciding what is copyrightable, which, they said, only the regional trial court may decide.
cases.issue: (1) May the Secretary of Justice reverse a finding of probable cause on a ground, the master tape, that was not raised during the preliminary investigation, and may he make a preliminary determination of what is copyrightable? (2) Is the format or mechanics of a television show protected by copyright? (3) Was the presentation of the master videotape necessary to determine probable cause?
cases.ruling: The Court dismissed the petition. (1) In reviewing a prosecutor's resolution, the Secretary of Justice is not precluded from considering errors, although unassigned, to determine whether there is probable cause; he must make his own finding and is not confined to the issues the parties raised, and his findings are not reviewable unless he committed grave abuse. Whether the format of a show is protected by copyright is a legal question for the court, but this does not prevent the Secretary from making a preliminary determination of it in deciding whether there is probable cause. (2) The format of a show is not copyrightable. Copyright is purely a statutory right, obtainable only for subjects that the statute enumerates, and Section 2 of P.D. No. 49, which is substantially the same as Section 172 of the Intellectual Property Code, does not list the format or mechanics of a television show. It refers to finished works, not concepts, and copyright does not extend to an idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept or principle (Section 175 of the Code). (3) BJPI's copyright covers the audio-visual recordings of each episode of Rhoda and Me, as cinematographic works under Section 2(M), not the general concept or format. For that reason the investigating prosecutor needed to compare the videotapes, and a mere written description of the formats was insufficient: the master videotape was indispensable to determining probable cause, because a television show includes more than words can describe.
cases.keyDoctrine: Copyright is purely statutory and protects only the classes of works the statute lists. It does not protect ideas, concepts, formats or mechanics, so the format of a television show is not copyrightable, and what is protected is the expression, such as the audio-visual recording of each episode. Because infringement is a matter of similarity between the works, the copyrighted work itself must usually be presented to determine probable cause.

cases.name: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Incorporated v. Shoemart, Incorporated and North Edsa Marketing, Incorporated
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. (P & D) makes advertising display units, called light boxes, which are illuminated by back lights and hold specially printed posters. It obtained a Certificate of Copyright Registration dated January 20, 1981 for these "Advertising Display Units", registered as a class "O" work under Section 2(O) of P.D. No. 49 (prints, pictorial illustrations, advertising copies, labels, tags and box wraps), and it registered the trademark "Poster Ads" in 1988, but only for stationeries such as letterheads, envelopes, calling cards and newsletters. It never obtained a patent for the light boxes. In 1985 it negotiated with Shoemart, Inc. (SMI) for the lease and installation of its light boxes in SM stores, but the deal collapsed. Later SMI had light boxes made, first by P & D's former manufacturer, Metro Industrial Services, and then by EYD Rainbow Advertising Corporation, some 300 units in 1991, and installed them in its stores, while North Edsa Marketing, Inc. (NEMI), a sister company, sold advertising space in them under "Poster Ads". P & D sued SMI and NEMI in 1991 for copyright and trademark infringement, unfair competition and damages. The Makati Regional Trial Court found both liable and awarded P & D P16.6 million in actual damages, plus moral and exemplary damages and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the copyright covered only the technical drawings and that "Poster Ads" was generic and registered only for stationeries. P & D went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: (1) If the engineering or technical drawings of an advertising light box are copyrighted, is the light box itself also protected by the copyright? (2) Is the light box protected only if it is also registered and patented? (3) Can the owner of a registered trademark prevent others from using it if the mark is a mere abbreviation of a term descriptive of its goods or business?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition and affirmed the Court of Appeals. (1) Copyright is purely statutory and covers only works within the statutory enumeration. P & D registered its copyright as a class "O" work, so its copyright extended only to the technical drawings (pictorial illustrations) and not to the light box, which is not a print, illustration, advertising copy, label, tag or box wrap, nor a literary or artistic work. If SMI had reprinted the drawings for sale, it would have infringed, but making units similar to the box drawn is not copying the drawings. (2) Trademark, copyright and patent are different rights that cannot be used interchangeably. P & D never secured a patent for the light boxes, and there can be no patent infringement without a patent: no patent, no protection. A copyright certificate is issued on a sworn ex parte claim without the scrutiny that a patent requires, and P & D could not obtain by copyright the exclusivity that it would have had to earn by a patent. Following Baker v. Selden, only the expression of an idea is protected by copyright, not the idea itself or the art that the work describes. (3) There was no trademark infringement. The certificate for "Poster Ads" specified only stationeries, which P & D did not even sell, so its exclusive right was limited to those goods, and registration for specific use on light boxes was an essential element that was missing. "Poster Ads" is also a generic contraction of "poster advertising" with no secondary meaning, as P & D's own expert admitted that it was too generic to identify any company. (4) Unfair competition was not found by the trial court and was not appealed by P & D, and in any case there was no evidence that the name was distinctive.
cases.keyDoctrine: Copyright, patent and trademark are distinct rights that cannot be used interchangeably. A copyright in technical drawings (a class "O" work) does not extend to the useful article drawn, and without a patent there is no protection against copying an invention (no patent, no protection). Copyright protects the expression, not the idea or the art it describes. A trademark registration gives an exclusive right only for the goods specified, and a generic term cannot be appropriated unless it acquires secondary meaning.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A foreign company's Philippine patent application was declared abandoned after its local agent failed to answer an office action from the patent office. Eight months after the date of abandonment, the company petitions to revive the application. It proves that its agent hid the office action from it, and it attaches a complete proposed response and pays every required fee. May the application be revived? Explain, based on E.I. Dupont de Nemours v. Director Francisco.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The application cannot be revived. The rules allow revival only within a short fixed period from the date of abandonment, and a petition filed after that period is out of time whatever the reason for the delay.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 113 of the 1962 Revised Rules of Practice, an abandoned application may be revived within four months from the date of abandonment, and an application not revived within the specified period is deemed forfeited. The later rules keep the four-month period (Rules 929 and 930 of the implementing rules), and Section 133.4 of the Intellectual Property Code provides a shorter period of three months. None of them gives an exception that could extend the period.
suggestedAnswer.application: The company filed its petition eight months after abandonment, which is later than four months and also later than three. The Court held that even if the delay was unavoidable, or the failure to prosecute was due to fraud, accident, mistake or excusable negligence, or the petition came with a complete proposed response and full payment of fees, the petition would still be denied because the regulations provide only a fixed period. So the agent's concealment, the proposed response and the fees do not help the company.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The application stays forfeited. Revival is not available after the period fixed by the rules, even for good cause.

keyPoints: An abandoned patent application may be revived only within a short fixed period from abandonment (four months under the old rules and the implementing rules; three months under Section 133.4 of the Intellectual Property Code)
No exception extends the period, even if the delay was unavoidable or due to fraud, accident, mistake or excusable negligence
A complete proposed response and payment of the fees do not cure a late petition
An application not revived in time is deemed forfeited

source.caseTitle: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
source.part: Part IV (the period for reviving an abandoned application)
source.excerpt: An abandoned patent application may only be revived within four (4) months from the date of abandonment. No extension of this period is provided by the 1962 Revised Rules of Practice. … Even if the delay was unavoidable, or the failure to prosecute was due to fraud, accident, mistake, or excusable negligence, or the Petition was accompanied by a complete proposed response, or all fees were paid, the Petition would still be denied since these regulations only provide a four (4 )- month period within which to file for the revival of the application. The rules do not provide any exception that could extend this four (4)-month period to 13 years.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A foreign inventor leaves all of its Philippine patent matters to one local lawyer. The lawyer dies. Years later the inventor learns of the death and appoints a new local agent, but it waits several more years before asking the patent office about its pending application, which turns out to have been declared abandoned long before. The inventor argues that it should not suffer for its deceased lawyer's failure to act. Is the inventor right? Explain, based on E.I. Dupont de Nemours v. Director Francisco.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The inventor is bound by its lawyer's negligence, and it was itself negligent, because a foreign client has a duty to keep itself informed about the progress of its local patent application.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Negligence is inexcusable if it could have been avoided through ordinary diligence and prudence, and the negligence of counsel binds the client. A foreign client may put its trust and confidence in its local resident agent, but it has a correlative duty to be diligent in keeping itself updated on its applications. As Bernardo v. Court of Appeals is quoted, no prudent party leaves the fate of its case entirely to its lawyer. In Schuartz v. Court of Appeals, applicants lost their patent applications because their counsel did not notice the notices of abandonment or revive within the period.
suggestedAnswer.application: The inventor asked for a status update only many years after filing. Even after it learned of its lawyer's death and replaced him, it waited years more before asking the patent office. Appointing a new agent did not revive the application: the power of attorney only told the office where to send notices on pending applications, and an application already abandoned and archived is not brought up again until a specific status update is requested. The inventor's own lack of prudence, together with its agent's negligence, caused the loss.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The inventor cannot disown its lawyer's conduct. Its negligence was inexcusable, so it cannot be relieved of the abandonment.

keyPoints: Negligence is inexcusable if ordinary diligence and prudence could have avoided it
The negligence of counsel binds the client
A foreign client has a correlative duty to keep itself updated on the progress of its local patent application
Appointing a new agent does not revive an application already abandoned and archived; the office acts only when a status update is requested
Schuartz v. Court of Appeals applies: applicants lose their rights when their counsel fails to notice abandonment and to revive in time

source.caseTitle: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
source.part: Part V (inexcusable negligence)
source.excerpt: Negligence is inexcusable if its commission could have been avoided through ordinary diligence and prudence. It is also settled that negligence of counsel binds the client … Although it was in petitioner's discretion as a foreign client to put its complete trust and confidence on its local resident agent, there was a correlative duty on its part to be diligent in keeping itself updated on the progress of its patent applications. Its failure to be informed of the abandonment of its patent application was caused by its own lack of prudence.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A foreign drug company applied for a patent in its home country, then applied in the Philippines within twelve months, claiming priority. The Philippine application was later declared abandoned and was never revived. A Philippine company now sells the same medicine locally. The foreign company argues that, because of its right of priority under the Paris Convention, the invention never became part of the public domain in the Philippines, and the local company must stop. Is it right? Explain, based on E.I. Dupont de Nemours v. Director Francisco.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A right of priority is not a patent. It gives no property right in the invention without an actual patent, and it has no bearing on the revival of an abandoned application.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 31 of the Intellectual Property Code, an applicant who earlier applied for the same invention in another country that gives Filipinos similar privileges is treated as having filed on the foreign filing date, if the Philippine application claims priority, is filed within twelve months and the required certified copy is filed in time. Under Section 29 (first to file), where two or more applications are filed for the same invention, the right to the patent belongs to the applicant with the earliest filing or priority date. So priority matters only when there are conflicting applications for the same invention. A right of priority does not automatically give a patent, and without a patent there is no protection.
suggestedAnswer.application: The local company has no conflicting patent application with the foreign company, so the priority date is irrelevant. The foreign company's application was abandoned and never revived, so there is no patent and no property right that can be enforced against the local company. If a right of priority were enough, a patent holder in any Paris Convention country would never need to apply for patents elsewhere.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The foreign company cannot stop the local company. Priority gives a preference between competing applicants; it does not replace a patent.

keyPoints: Section 31: a foreign filing date can be claimed if the Philippine application claims priority, is filed within twelve months and the certified copy is filed in time
Section 29 (first to file): between conflicting applications for the same invention, the earliest filing or priority date prevails
A right of priority is relevant only when two or more applications conflict
A right of priority is not equivalent to a patent and gives no property rights in the absence of an actual patent
Priority has no bearing on the revival of an abandoned application

source.caseTitle: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
source.part: Part VI (right of priority)
source.excerpt: The right of priority given to a patent applicant is only relevant when there are two or more conflicting patent applications on the same invention. Because a right of priority does not automatically grant letters patent to an applicant, possession of a right of priority does not confer any property rights on the applicant in the absence of an actual patent. … However, this right of priority does not immediately entitle a patent applicant the grant of a patent. A right of priority is not equivalent to a patent. Otherwise, a patent holder of any member-state of the Paris Convention need not apply for patents in other countries where it wishes to exercise its patent.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: The procedural rules of an intellectual property office say that proceedings to revive a patent application are strictly between the examiner and the applicant, and they do not allow third parties to intervene. On appeal to the Court of Appeals, a competitor asks to intervene. Under E.I. Dupont de Nemours v. Director Francisco, which statement is correct?

choices.A: The prohibition binds the Court of Appeals too, because the appeal is a continuation of the same proceeding.
choices.B: The Court of Appeals may never allow intervention in an appeal from an administrative agency.
choices.C: The prohibition applies only to proceedings before the agency; in the Court of Appeals, the Rules of Court decide whether the competitor may intervene.
choices.D: The competitor may intervene as a matter of right once the appeal is filed, and the Court of Appeals has no discretion.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court held that an agency's procedural rules govern only proceedings within the agency. Once the matter is before the Court of Appeals, the Rules of Court apply, and Rule 19 gives the court discretion to decide whether to give due course to an intervention. The court asks whether the intervenor has a legal interest, whether the intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the rights of the original parties, and whether its rights can be protected in a separate proceeding. A is wrong because any earlier prohibition on intervention does not apply in the Court of Appeals. B is wrong because the Court of Appeals has discretion under Rule 19 and may allow intervention. D is wrong because intervention is a matter of the court's sound discretion, not a matter of right.

source.caseTitle: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
source.part: Part III (intervention before the Court of Appeals)
source.excerpt: Rule 19 of the Rules of Court provides that a court has the discretion to determine whether to give due course to an intervention. … If an administrative agency's procedural rules expressly prohibit an intervention by third parties, the prohibition is limited only to the proceedings before the administrative agency. Once the matter is brought before the Court of Appeals in a petition for review, any prior prohibition on intervention does not apply since the only question to be determined is whether the intervenor has established a right to intervene under the Rules of Court.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In an appeal from an intellectual property office, the Court of Appeals allows a competitor to intervene and then decides the case on the merits against the applicant. The applicant wants to challenge both rulings before the Supreme Court. According to E.I. Dupont de Nemours v. Director Francisco, what is the proper remedy?

choices.A: A petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45, because the Court of Appeals has already resolved both the intervention and the merits.
choices.B: A special civil action of certiorari under Rule 65, because the grant of intervention is an interlocutory order.
choices.C: A special civil action of certiorari under Rule 65 first, and only after it is decided, a petition under Rule 45.
choices.D: A motion for reconsideration before the Director General of the intellectual property office.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Intervention results in an interlocutory order, which is generally reviewable only by certiorari under Rule 65 on a clear showing of grave abuse of discretion. But when the Court of Appeals has already resolved the intervention and the merits of the case, an appeal by petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 is the proper remedy. Rule 65 corrects errors of jurisdiction, while Rule 45 is a mode of appeal that corrects errors of judgment, and whether intervention is proper is a question of law. B describes the usual route when only the interlocutory order is challenged, which is not this situation. C is wrong because the Court did not require two petitions in sequence. D is wrong because the case had already gone past the intellectual property office to the Court of Appeals.

source.caseTitle: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
source.part: Part I (the proper mode of appeal)
source.excerpt: However, when the Court of Appeals has already resolved the question of intervention and the merits of the case, an appeal through a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court is the proper remedy. … The special civil action of certiorari under Rule 65 is intended to correct errors of jurisdiction. … A petition for review under Rule 45, on the other hand, is a mode of appeal intended to correct errors of judgment.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In E.I. Dupont de Nemours v. Director Francisco, the Court stressed that a patent holder of an invention relating to food or medicine does not enjoy an absolute monopoly. Under Republic Act No. 165, as the decision discusses it, when may a compulsory license be granted to an applicant for such an invention if it is necessary for public health or safety?

choices.A: At any time after the patent application is filed.
choices.B: One year after the patent is granted.
choices.C: Ten years after the patent is granted.
choices.D: Three years after the grant of the patent.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The decision states that under Republic Act No. 165 a compulsory license may be granted to any applicant three years after the grant of a patent if the invention relates to food or medicine necessary for public health or safety. Quoting Smith Kline & French Laboratories v. Court of Appeals, it explains that the aim was not only to let others supply the public with the patented product but also to prevent the growth of monopolies, and the patentee is not deprived of all rights because he enjoys three years of complete monopoly and then a licensing agreement with a reasonable royalty. A, B and C do not match the period stated in the decision. Watch for: this is the rule of Republic Act No. 165 as quoted in the decision; compulsory licensing is now governed by the Intellectual Property Code, so check its current text.

source.caseTitle: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
source.part: Part VII (limits on a patent holder's monopoly, compulsory licensing)
source.excerpt: Under Republic Act No. 165, a compulsory license may be granted to any applicant three (3) years after the grant of a patent if the invention relates to food or medicine necessary for public health or safety. … In the explanatory note of Bill No. 1156 which eventually became R.A. No. 165, the legislative intent in the grant of a compulsory license was not only to afford others an opportunity to provide the public with the quantity of the patented product, but also to prevent the growth of monopolies.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Company X files its Philippine patent application for a process on March 1. Company Y, which independently made the same invention, had filed for it in Japan on January 10 of the same year, and then filed in the Philippines on May 20, expressly claiming priority and filing the required certified copy in time. Japan gives Filipinos similar privileges. Under the first-to-file and priority provisions quoted in E.I. Dupont de Nemours v. Director Francisco, who has the better right to the patent?

choices.A: Company X, because it filed first in the Philippines.
choices.B: Company Y, because its application is considered filed on January 10, the earliest priority date.
choices.C: Whichever company first started using the process in the Philippines.
choices.D: Both equally, because each filed an application for the same invention.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Section 31 of the Intellectual Property Code treats an application by a person who has previously applied for the same invention in another country that gives Filipinos similar privileges as filed on the date of the foreign application, provided the local application expressly claims priority, is filed within twelve months of the earliest foreign filing, and the certified copy and English translation are filed within six months. Company Y met those conditions, so its application counts as filed on January 10. Under Section 29, where two or more applications are filed for the same invention, the right belongs to the applicant with the earliest filing date or the earliest priority date, which is Company Y. A is wrong because the Philippine filing date is not the only date that counts. C is wrong because the test is the filing or priority date, not first use. D is wrong because the right to the patent belongs to one applicant. Watch for: a right of priority only decides between conflicting applications; it is not itself a patent.

source.caseTitle: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
source.part: Part VI (Sections 31 and 29 of the Intellectual Property Code)
source.excerpt: SECTION 31. Right of Priority. - An application for patent filed by any person who has previously applied for the same invention in another country which by treaty, convention, or law affords similar privileges to Filipino citizens, shall be considered as filed as of the date of filing the foreign application: … SECTION 29. First to File Rule. - If two (2) or more persons have made the invention separately and independently of each other, the right to the patent shall belong to the person who filed an application for such invention, or where two or more applications are filed for the same invention, to the applicant who has the earliest filing date or, the earliest priority date.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In E.I. Dupont de Nemours v. Director Francisco, the Court described the three-fold purpose of patent law. Which of the following is one of those purposes?

choices.A: To let an inventor keep an invention secret and still enjoy protection indefinitely.
choices.B: To make patents easy to obtain so that as many ideas as possible are protected.
choices.C: To promote the disclosure of inventions, so that the public may practice them once the patent expires.
choices.D: To keep ideas that are already in the public domain out of the public's reach.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court quoted the three purposes: first, to foster and reward invention; second, to promote disclosure of inventions to stimulate further innovation and to permit the public to practice the invention once the patent expires; third, the stringent requirements for patent protection ensure that ideas in the public domain remain there for the free use of the public. A is wrong because the bargain is exclusive rights for a limited period in return for disclosure, and an inventor who keeps the invention secret is not protected by a patent. B is wrong because the requirements are strict, not easy. D is the opposite of the third purpose, which keeps public domain ideas free for everyone to use.

source.caseTitle: E.I. Dupont de Nemours and Co. v. Director Emma C. Francisco, et al.
source.part: Part VII (the purpose of the patent system)
source.excerpt: The patent law has a three-fold purpose: "first, patent law seeks to foster and reward invention; second, it promotes disclosures of inventions to stimulate further innovation and to permit the public to practice the invention once the patent expires; third, the stringent requirements for patent protection. seek to ensure that ideas in the public domain remain there for the free use of the public."

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company holds a patent whose claims describe only a chemical compound called Compound A and ways of using it. A competitor sells a product whose active ingredient is Compound B, a differently named compound that appears nowhere in the patent. The patent holder sues for infringement, arguing that Compound B is covered, but its only evidence is the patent itself and the testimony of its own sales manager. Will the suit prosper? Explain, based on Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The patent holder has the burden of proving infringement, and a patent covers only what its claims say. Nothing in the claims mentions Compound B, and the patent holder offered no competent evidence that its patent embraces it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The burden of proof to substantiate a charge of patent infringement rests on the plaintiff. When the language of the claims is clear and distinct, the patentee is bound by it and may not claim anything beyond it; courts may not add to or detract from the claims matters not expressed or necessarily implied, nor enlarge the patent beyond what the inventor claimed and the patent office allowed. The mere absence of a compound's name from the patent is not determinative of its non-inclusion, but then extrinsic evidence is needed to show that the compound inheres in the patent or that the meaning of the claims embraces it.
suggestedAnswer.application: The claims describe Compound A and its uses and say nothing about Compound B. The patent holder's evidence consists of the patent and its own sales manager's testimony. The manager was not qualified as an expert with knowledge of chemical compounds, so the testimony does not prove that Compound B is within the claims. Without extrinsic proof that Compound B inheres in the patent, the claims, being clear, cannot be stretched to cover it.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The infringement suit fails because the patent holder did not carry its burden of proof.

keyPoints: The burden of proving patent infringement rests on the plaintiff
A patentee is bound by the clear language of its claims and may not claim anything beyond them
Courts may not enlarge the patent beyond what the inventor claimed and the patent office allowed
The absence of a compound's name is not by itself determinative, but extrinsic evidence is then needed to show the claims embrace it
A witness who is not qualified as an expert cannot prove that two chemical compounds are the same

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the principal issue (patent infringement)
source.excerpt: The burden of proof to substantiate a charge for patent infringement rests on the plaintiff. … When the language of its claims is clear and distinct, the patentee is bound thereby and may not claim anything beyond them. And so are the courts bound which may not add to or detract from the claims matters not expressed or necessarily implied, nor may they enlarge the patent beyond the scope of that which the inventor claimed and the patent office allowed, even if the patentee may have been entitled to something more than the words it had chosen would include. … The testimony of Dr. Orinion lends no support to petitioner’s cause, he not having been presented or qualified as an expert witness who has the knowledge or expertise on the matter of chemical compounds.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent covers a water filter that removes impurities through a three-stage mechanical process. A competitor sells a filter that also removes impurities and works just as well, but it does so chemically, by a different means. The patent holder invokes the doctrine of equivalents. Will the doctrine apply? Explain, based on Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Reaching the same result is not enough. Under the doctrine of equivalents the competing device must perform substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, and the patent holder must prove all three. Here the means are different.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The doctrine of equivalents provides that infringement also takes place when a device appropriates a prior invention by incorporating its innovative concept and, although with some modification and change, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. It requires satisfaction of the function-means-and-result test, and the patentee has the burden to show that all three components are met. Identity of result does not amount to infringement unless the other device operates in substantially the same way or by substantially the same means; the principle or mode of operation must be the same or substantially the same.
suggestedAnswer.application: Both filters remove impurities, so the function and the result are similar. But the competitor's filter removes them chemically, while the patented filter does so through a three-stage mechanical process. The means or mode of operation is therefore not substantially the same, and the patent holder cannot satisfy the middle part of the test. It also has the burden of showing, with competent evidence, how the competing filter works.
