suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The doctrine of equivalents does not apply, and the competitor does not infringe on that theory.

keyPoints: Doctrine of equivalents: substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result
The function-means-and-result test has three parts, and the patentee must prove all three
Identity of result alone is not infringement; the principle or mode of operation must be the same or substantially the same
The patentee has the burden of proof, and unqualified testimony does not prove equivalence

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the doctrine of equivalents
source.excerpt: The doctrine of equivalents provides that an infringement also takes place when a device appropriates a prior invention by incorporating its innovative concept and, although with some modification and change, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. … While both compounds have the effect of neutralizing parasites in animals, identity of result does not amount to infringement of patent unless Albendazole operates in substantially the same way or by substantially the same means as the patented compound, even though it performs the same function and achieves the same result. In other words, the principle or mode of operation must be the same or substantially the same. The doctrine of equivalents thus requires satisfaction of the function-means-and-result test, the patentee having the burden to show that all three components of such equivalency test are met.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company's patent was granted on a divisional application split off from an earlier application that claimed two inventions, Invention One and Invention Two. The patent claims only Invention Two. The company sues a competitor that sells a product made with Invention One, arguing that because both inventions started in the same original application, Invention One is also covered by its patent. Is the company right? Explain, based on Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A divisional application shows that the claimed invention is distinct from the other inventions in the original application. It does not extend the resulting patent to those other inventions.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A divisional application comes into play when two or more inventions are claimed in a single application but are of such a nature that a single patent may not be issued for them. The applicant is required to divide, that is, to limit the claims to whichever invention he elects, and the inventions not elected may be made the subject of separate applications, called divisional applications.
suggestedAnswer.application: The company's patent came from a divisional application. If a single patent could have covered both Invention One and Invention Two, there would have been no need for a divisional application. So the very fact that the patent was issued on a divisional application means that Invention Two is an invention distinct from Invention One. The patent covers Invention Two only, and the claims are what bind the patentee.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The company cannot claim Invention One under this patent, and the argument based on the divisional application fails.

keyPoints: A divisional application is used when two or more inventions are claimed in one application and a single patent cannot be issued for them
The applicant limits the claims to the invention elected; the others may be the subject of separate applications
An invention issued on a divisional application is distinct from the other inventions in the original application
Sharing an original application does not make the other inventions part of the resulting patent

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of divisional applications
source.excerpt: As for the concept of divisional applications proffered by petitioner, it comes into play when two or more inventions are claimed in a single application but are of such a nature that a single patent may not be issued for them. The applicant thus is required "to divide," that is, to limit the claims to whichever invention he may elect, whereas those inventions not elected may be made the subject of separate applications which are called "divisional applications." What this only means is that petitioner’s methyl 5 propylthio-2-benzimidazole carbamate is an invention distinct from the other inventions claimed in the original application divided out, Albendazole being one of those other inventions.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent holder appeals to the Supreme Court by petition for review on certiorari from a Court of Appeals decision that found no infringement. In its petition it asks the Court to re-weigh the evidence on whether the two products are the same. According to Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals, what is the general rule?

choices.A: The Supreme Court re-weighs the evidence in every petition for review on certiorari.
choices.B: Only questions of law may be raised, and the Court does not review the appellate court's factual findings unless, for example, they are mistaken, absurd, speculative, conjectural or contrary to the findings of the court of origin.
choices.C: Only questions of fact may be raised, because patent cases are technical.
choices.D: The Court must adopt the findings of the trial court even if the Court of Appeals reached a different conclusion.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court repeated that only questions of law may be raised in a petition for review on certiorari, and that it does not review the appellate court's factual findings unless they are mistaken, absurd, speculative, conjectural, conflicting, tainted with grave abuse of discretion, or contrary to the findings culled by the court of origin. After examining the record, it found nothing wrong in the appellate court's conclusions on infringement. A is wrong because the Court is not a trier of facts. C is the opposite of the rule. D is wrong because the stated exceptions concern the appellate court's findings being, among other things, contrary to those of the court of origin; the rule does not bind the Court to the trial court in every case.

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the principal issue (the Court's power of review)
source.excerpt: As has repeatedly been held, only questions of law may be raised in a petition for review on certiorari before this Court. Unless the factual findings of the appellate court are mistaken, absurd, speculative, conjectural, conflicting, tainted with grave abuse of discretion, or contrary to the findings culled by the court of origin, this Court does not review them.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent's claims describe only one chemical compound by name. The patent holder sues a competitor whose drug contains a different, differently named compound, arguing that the patent covers it too. According to Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals, what is the effect of the second compound's name not appearing anywhere in the patent?

choices.A: It is conclusive that the compound is outside the patent, and no further evidence may be received.
choices.B: It is conclusive that the compound is inside the patent, because every patent includes all related compounds.
choices.C: It makes the patent void for failing to describe the invention.
choices.D: It is not determinative by itself, but the patent holder must then present extrinsic evidence that the compound inheres in the patent or that the meaning of the claims embraces it.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court stressed that the mere absence of the word Albendazole from the patent is not determinative of Albendazole's non-inclusion in the claims. But the language of the patent yielded nothing about Albendazole, and no extrinsic evidence was adduced to prove that it inheres in the patent despite its omission or that the meaning of the claims embraces it. So the patent holder lost. A is wrong because the Court did not treat the omission as conclusive. B is wrong because a patent does not automatically include related compounds; the patentee is bound by its claims. C is wrong because nothing in the decision links the omission to the validity of the patent.

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the principal issue (the claims of the patent)
source.excerpt: It bears stressing that the mere absence of the word Albendazole in Letters Patent No. 14561 is not determinative of Albendazole’s non-inclusion in the claims of the patent. While Albendazole is admittedly a chemical compound that exists by a name different from that covered in petitioner’s letters patent, the language of Letter Patent No. 14561 fails to yield anything at all regarding Albendazole. And no extrinsic evidence had been adduced to prove that Albendazole inheres in petitioner’s patent in spite of its omission therefrom or that the meaning of the claims of the patent embraces the same.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent holder shows that a competitor's substance kills the same parasites as its patented substance, so that both perform the same function and achieve the same result. According to Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals, what more must the patent holder prove to establish infringement under the doctrine of equivalents?

choices.A: That the competing substance operates in substantially the same way or by substantially the same means as the patented substance.
choices.B: That the competing substance is cheaper than the patented substance.
choices.C: That the competing substance was sold only after the patent was granted.
choices.D: Nothing more, because identity of function and result is enough.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The doctrine of equivalents requires the function-means-and-result test, and the patentee has the burden of showing that all three components are met. The Court said that identity of result does not amount to infringement unless the other substance operates in substantially the same way or by substantially the same means, even though it performs the same function and achieves the same result: the principle or mode of operation must be the same or substantially the same. B and C have nothing to do with the test. D is wrong because the Court rejected the idea that equal function and result alone are enough.

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the doctrine of equivalents
source.excerpt: While both compounds have the effect of neutralizing parasites in animals, identity of result does not amount to infringement of patent unless Albendazole operates in substantially the same way or by substantially the same means as the patented compound, even though it performs the same function and achieves the same result. In other words, the principle or mode of operation must be the same or substantially the same.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: After a court's injunction stopped its sales, a company claims lost profits as actual damages. It proves the amount only through its President and Executive Vice-President, who testify that monthly sales had been P100,000 and fell to zero. According to Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals, how should the claim be treated?

choices.A: It should be granted in full, because lost profits are always presumed after an injunction.
choices.B: It should be granted, because officers of a company are the best witnesses of its sales.
choices.C: It should be denied as actual damages, because the officers' testimony is not competent proof or the best evidence obtainable; documentary evidence is also required, though temperate damages may be awarded for a pecuniary loss that cannot be proved with certainty.
choices.D: It should be denied, and no damages of any kind may be awarded.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Actual or compensatory damages cover not only the loss suffered but also profits the injured party failed to obtain, but the actual amount must be proved with a reasonable degree of certainty, based on competent proof and the best evidence obtainable. The officers' testimonies were not the competent proof or best evidence, because such damages also require documentary evidence. The Court therefore deleted the P330,000 actual damages. It instead awarded P20,000 as temperate or moderate damages, because the company had suffered some pecuniary loss the amount of which could not, from the nature of the case, be established with certainty. A and B are wrong because the amount of damages is not presumed or established by officers' say-so alone. D is wrong because the Court did award temperate damages.

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the awards of actual and temperate damages
source.excerpt: While indemnification for actual or compensatory damages covers not only the loss suffered (damnum emergens) but also profits which the obligee failed to obtain (lucrum cessans or ganacias frustradas), it is necessary to prove the actual amount of damages with a reasonable degree of certainty based on competent proof and on the best evidence obtainable by the injured party. The testimonies of private respondent’s officers are not the competent proof or best evidence obtainable to establish its right to actual or compensatory damages for such damages also require presentation of documentary evidence to substantiate a claim therefor. … This Court, however, grants private respondent temperate or moderate damages in the amount of ₱20,000.00 which it finds reasonable under the circumstances, it having suffered some pecuniary loss the amount of which cannot, from the nature of the case, be established with certainty.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company is sued for patent infringement and wins. It asks for attorney's fees, arguing that it was forced to litigate to protect its rights, but there is no evidence that the patent holder acted with malice. According to Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals, should attorney's fees be awarded?

choices.A: Yes, because being forced to litigate always entitles a winning party to attorney's fees.
choices.B: No, because even if a party is compelled to litigate to protect its rights, attorney's fees may not be awarded without sufficient showing of bad faith, and persistence in a case out of an erroneous conviction of the righteousness of one's cause is not bad faith.
choices.C: Yes, because the patent holder lost the case.
choices.D: Yes, because attorney's fees are automatically awarded in every patent case.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court deleted the attorney's fees that the Court of Appeals had granted under Article 2208 (2) of the Civil Code. Even if a claimant is compelled to litigate with third persons or to incur expenses to protect its rights, attorney's fees may not be awarded where no sufficient showing of bad faith is reflected in a party's persistence in a case other than an erroneous conviction of the righteousness of his cause, and there was no evidence that the patent holder was moved by malice. A is wrong because being forced to litigate is not enough by itself. C is wrong because losing a case is not bad faith. D is wrong because nothing in the decision makes attorney's fees automatic.

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the award of attorney's fees
source.excerpt: Even if a claimant is compelled to litigate with third persons or to incur expenses to protect its rights, still attorney’s fees may not be awarded where no sufficient showing of bad faith could be reflected in a party’s persistence in a case other than an erroneous conviction of the righteousness of his cause. There exists no evidence on record indicating that petitioner was moved by malice in suing private respondent.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent claims a hand tractor with a list of specific parts: a circular floating housing, a front wheel, a protective water covering, a transmission box, a V-shaped inclined handle and an engine base on top of the housing. The patent holder sues a shop owner whose hand tractors, when placed side by side with the patented one and photographed from every angle, have the same parts in the same arrangement and, as the shop owner admits, operate on the same principles. How should a court decide whether there is infringement under the first test of infringement, and what is the likely result? Explain, based on Godines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The court applies the test of literal infringement. It looks first to the words of the claims and compares them with the accused product. Because the shop owner's tractors have all the material elements of the claims, the likely result is a finding of infringement.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The tests of infringement are (a) literal infringement and (b) the doctrine of equivalents. In literal infringement, resort must be had, in the first instance, to the words of the claim, and if the accused matter clearly falls within the claim, infringement is made out and that is the end of it. To decide this, the court must juxtapose the claims of the patent and the accused product within the overall context of the claims and specifications to see whether there is exact identity of all material elements.
suggestedAnswer.application: The court compares the listed parts of the claim with the shop owner's tractors, element by element, and may inspect samples placed alongside the patented one. Here the form, configuration, design and appearance are the same, the parts are virtually the same, and the shop owner himself admits that the two operate on the same principles. The claims and the features of the patented model were evidently copied, so the accused product falls within the claims.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: There is literal infringement, and the shop owner is liable to the patent holder.

keyPoints: Two tests of infringement: literal infringement and the doctrine of equivalents
In literal infringement, resort first to the words of the claim; if the accused matter clearly falls within the claim, infringement is made out
The court juxtaposes the claims and the accused product, within the context of the claims and specifications, to see whether there is exact identity of all material elements
Inspection of samples, similarity of parts and admission that they operate on the same principles support a finding of copying

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the tests of infringement and the trial court's comparison of the tillers
source.excerpt: Tests have been established to determine infringement. These are (a) literal infringement; and (b) the doctrine of equivalents. In using literal infringement as a test, ". . . resort must be had, in the first instance, to the words of the claim. If accused matter clearly falls within the claim, infringement is made out and that is the end of it." To determine whether the particular item falls within the literal meaning of the patent claims, the court must juxtapose the claims of the patent and the accused product within the overall context of the claims and specifications, to determine whether there is exact identity of all material elements. … Viewed from any perspective or angle, the power tiller of the defendant is identical and similar to that of the turtle power tiller of plaintiff in form, configuration, design and appearance. The parts or components thereof are virtually the same. … It appears from the foregoing observation of the trial court that these claims of the patent and the features of the patented utility model were copied by petitioner. We are compelled to arrive at no other conclusion but that there was infringement.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A shop owner copies a patented machine but changes its name, makes the housing a little rounder and moves a handle a few centimeters. When sued for infringement, he argues that his machine is different from the patented one, so there is no literal infringement. Is the argument a good defense? Explain, based on Godines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Under the doctrine of equivalents, minor modifications do not put a copy beyond the reach of the patent. A device that does substantially the same work in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result infringes, even if it differs in name, form or shape.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Courts adopted the doctrine of equivalents because the logical fallback of a defendant is to say that his product is different. Under it, an infringement also occurs when a device appropriates a prior invention by incorporating its innovative concept and, albeit with some modification and change, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. The reason for the doctrine is that allowing the imitation of a patented invention that copies no literal detail would turn the protection of the patent into a hollow and useless thing and would encourage the unscrupulous copyist to make unimportant and insubstantial changes that take the copy outside the claim.
suggestedAnswer.application: The shop owner changed only the name, the roundness of the housing and the position of a handle. Those are unimportant and insubstantial changes. What matters is what the elements do, so the court asks whether the machine performs the same function in substantially the same way and reaches substantially the same result. If so, then differences in name, form or shape are immaterial.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The defense fails. The shop owner infringes the patent under the doctrine of equivalents even though there is no literal copy.

keyPoints: Doctrine of equivalents: infringement occurs when a device, with some modification, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result
Minor modifications do not take a copy outside the patent
Reason: otherwise the patent's protection would be hollow, and unscrupulous copyists would make insubstantial changes
Similarities and differences are judged by what the elements do, not by names; differences of form or name are immaterial

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the doctrine of equivalents
source.excerpt: Recognizing that the logical fallback position of one in the place of defendant is to aver that his product is different from the patented one, courts have adopted the doctrine of equivalents which recognizes that minor modifications in a patented invention are sufficient to put the item beyond the scope of literal infringement. Thus, according to this doctrine, "(a)n infringement also occurs when a device appropriates a prior invention by incorporating its innovative concept and, albeit with some modification and change, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result." The reason for the doctrine of equivalents is that to permit the imitation of a patented invention which does not copy any literal detail would be to convert the protection of the patent grant into a hollow and useless thing. Such imitation would leave room for — indeed encourage — the unscrupulous copyist to make unimportant and insubstantial changes and substitutions in the patent which, though adding nothing, would be enough to take the copied matter outside the claim, and hence outside the reach of the law.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A machine shop owner is sued for making and selling copies of a patented machine. He says that he never made machines on his own design, but only on special order, following his customers' own specifications. The courts find that he had been making and selling similar machines long before the patent holder sold its own, that he has no job orders to show, and that it would be unusual for buyers to order such machines on verbal instructions alone. May he re-argue the point before the Supreme Court on a petition for review, and does his defense succeed? Explain, based on Godines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No to both. Whether he made and sold the machines is a question of fact that the Supreme Court does not re-examine on a petition for review, and the courts' reasons for rejecting his defense are sound.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 is limited to errors of law, and the findings of fact of the Court of Appeals are conclusive upon it. Whether the petitioner was manufacturing and selling the items is a question of fact better addressed to the lower courts.
suggestedAnswer.application: The trial court found the defense untenable because (1) the shop owner admitted in his Answer that he had been making and selling such machines long before the patent holder started selling its own, which showed that he was principally a manufacturer working on his own specifications and designs; (2) he showed no job orders, although it would be unbelievable for him to make copies without them, especially since he is an engineer and owns the shop; and (3) it is contrary to usual business practice, and costly and time-consuming, for buyers to order machines on verbal instructions alone. The courts therefore established that he made and sold the machines without the patentee's authority.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: He cannot re-argue the fact, and his defense fails. He made and sold the machines without authority.

keyPoints: A petition for review under Rule 45 is limited to errors of law; the findings of fact of the Court of Appeals are conclusive
Whether the accused manufactured and sold the items is a question of fact for the lower courts
No job orders were presented, and it would be unusual to make copies without specifications or to order them on verbal instructions
His admission of long-time manufacturing and selling showed that he made the machines on his own design
Making and selling without the patentee's authority was established

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of whether petitioner manufactured and sold the tillers
source.excerpt: The question of whether petitioner was manufacturing and selling power tillers is a question of fact better addressed to the lower courts. … However, this contention appears untenable in the light of the following circumstances: 1) he admits in his Answer that he has been manufacturing power tillers or hand tractors, selling and distributing them long before plaintiff started selling its turtle power tiller in Zamboanga del Sur and Misamis Occidental, meaning that defendant is principally a manufacturer of power tillers, not upon specification and design of buyers, but upon his own specification and design; 2) it would be unbelievable that defendant would fabricate power tillers similar to the turtle power tillers of plaintiff upon specifications of buyers without requiring a job order where the specification and designs of those ordered are specified. No document was (sic) ever been presented showing such job orders, and it is rather unusual for defendant to manufacture something without the specification and designs, considering that he is an engineer by profession and proprietor of the Ozamis Engineering shop. … Of general acceptance is the rule imbedded in our jurisprudence that ". . . the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in cases brought to it from the Court of Appeals in a petition for certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court is limited to the review of errors of law, and that said appellate court's findings of fact are conclusive upon this Court." … The fact that petitioner herein manufactured and sold power tillers without patentee's authority has been established by the courts despite petitioner's claims to the contrary.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under Section 37 of Republic Act No. 165, as applied in Godines v. Court of Appeals, which act is an infringement of a patent?

choices.A: Selling an unpatented product that is similar in function to the patented one.
choices.B: Studying the patented machine in a classroom without selling anything.
choices.C: Making, using or selling the patented machine without the patentee's authorization.
choices.D: Publishing the patent in a newspaper of general circulation.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Section 37, as quoted in the decision, gives the patentee the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented machine, article or product, and to use the patented process for the purpose of industry or commerce, throughout the Philippines for the term of the patent, and says that such making, using or selling by any person without the patentee's authorization constitutes infringement. A is wrong because a product that does not fall within the claims, literally or by equivalents, does not infringe; similarity of function alone is not the test. B is wrong because the section speaks of making, using or selling for the purpose of industry or commerce, not of studying. D is wrong because publication of the patent was something SV-Agro did, not an act of infringement. Watch for: this is the provision of the old Patent Law (Republic Act No. 165) applied in the decision; patents are now governed by the Intellectual Property Code, so check its current text.
