source.part: The Ruling of this Court (the second reason: the Paris Convention and well-known marks)
source.excerpt: Thus, this Court has ruled that the Philippines is obligated to assure nationals of countries of the Paris Convention that they are afforded an effective protection against violation of their intellectual property rights in the Philippines in the same way that their own countries are obligated to accord similar protection to Philippine nationals. … To be protected under the two directives of the Ministry of Trade, an internationally well-known mark need not be registered or used in the Philippines. All that is required is that the mark is well-known internationally and in the Philippines for identical or similar goods, whether or not the mark is registered or used in the Philippines. … Rule 102. Criteria for determining whether a mark is well-known. In determining whether a mark is well-known, the following criteria or any combination thereof may be taken into account: … (e) the extent to which the mark has been registered in the world; … As such, even before Harvard University applied for registration of the mark "Harvard" in the Philippines, the mark was already protected under Article 6bis and Article 8 of the Paris Convention.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A local clothing company registers the name of a famous foreign university as its brand. Its logo also carries the words "Established 1936", "USA" and the university's city, although the company has no connection with the university, the city or the United States. The company later says that it used these words only "to evoke a lifestyle". May the registration stand? Explain, based on Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The registration should not have been allowed, because the mark falsely suggests a connection with the university. Section 4(a) of the Trademark Law prohibits the registration of such a mark, and the violation is a ground for cancellation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 4(a) of R.A. No. 166 prohibits the registration of a mark that consists of or comprises matter that may disparage or falsely suggest a connection with persons, living or dead, institutions, beliefs or national symbols. The provision is identical to Section 2(a) of the Lanham Act of the United States and is intended to protect the right of publicity of famous individuals and institutions from the commercial exploitation of their goodwill by others. Under Section 17(c) of R.A. No. 166, a registration obtained in violation of Section 4 may be cancelled.
suggestedAnswer.application: The company has no affiliation with the university or its city, and it was not established in 1936 or in the United States, yet its logo combines the university's name with these words. That obviously suggests a false connection with the university. The company's belated explanation that it wished to evoke a lifestyle or a desirable aura only confirms that it sought to connect its products with the university and to ride on its prestige and popularity, appropriating part of its goodwill without its consent. That is exactly the commercial exploitation of goodwill that Section 4(a) forbids.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The registration should have been disallowed, and the violation of Section 4(a) is a ground for cancelling it under Section 17(c).

keyPoints: Section 4(a) of R.A. No. 166 prohibits registering a mark that may falsely suggest a connection with persons, institutions, beliefs or national symbols
Use of the famous name together with a claimed origin in the university's city and "Established 1936" and "USA" suggests a false connection
The provision protects the right of publicity of famous individuals and institutions against exploitation of their goodwill
A belated justification of evoking a desirable aura confirms the intent to connect the products with the university
Under Section 17(c), a registration obtained in violation of Section 4 is a ground for cancellation

No. 166 prohibits the registration of a mark "which may disparage or falsely suggest a connection with persons, living or dead, institutions, beliefs x x x." … Fredco’s use of the mark "Harvard," coupled with its claimed origin in Cambridge, Massachusetts, obviously suggests a false connection with Harvard University. On this ground alone, Fredco’s registration of the mark "Harvard" should have been disallowed. … Section 4(a) of R.A. No. 166 is identical to Section 2(a) of the Lanham Act, the trademark law of the United States. These provisions are intended to protect the right of publicity of famous individuals and institutions from commercial exploitation of their goodwill by others. … Under Section 17(c) of R.A. No. 166, such violation is a ground for cancellation of Fredco’s registration of the mark "Harvard" because the registration was obtained in violation of Section 4 of R.A. No. 166.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A foreign company registered its mark at home and then obtained a Philippine registration based on that home registration, without ever having used the mark in the Philippines. A local company that began using a similar mark in the Philippines earlier argues that its earlier actual use in the Philippines should prevail. Is the argument correct? Explain, based on Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A registration based on a home registration in a Paris Convention country does not require actual prior use of the mark in the Philippines, and any such defect was in any case cured by the Intellectual Property Code.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 2 of R.A. No. 166 requires, for the registration of a trademark, proof that it has actually been used in commerce in the Philippines for not less than two months before the application, but where the mark is already registered in a foreign country that is a member of the Paris Convention, that proof is not necessary, because Section 37 allows registration on the basis of a home registration. An applicant on a home registration need not even have used the mark in the country. Under Section 239.2 of R.A. No. 8293, marks registered under R.A. No. 166 remain in force but are deemed to have been granted under the new Code, which does not require actual prior use in the Philippines.
suggestedAnswer.application: The foreign company's registration rested on home registration, so its lack of prior use in the Philippines does not defeat it. Its registration is now deemed granted under the Intellectual Property Code, which does not require prior use here, so any defect arising from the absence of actual use in the Philippines has been cured. The local company's earlier use does not prevail. In the decision itself, the local claimant's own registration had been cancelled for failure to file the affidavit of use on the fifth anniversary, so it was no longer the registrant or presumptive owner.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The local company's argument fails, and the foreign company's registration is not defeated by the lack of actual use in the Philippines.

That proof is not necessary when the mark is registered in a foreign country that is a member of the Paris Convention (home registration, Section 37)
Under Section 239.2 of R.A. No. 8293, marks registered under R.A. No. 166 are deemed granted under the Code, which does not require actual prior use in the Philippines
Any defect from lack of prior use in the Philippines was cured by Section 239.2
A registration cancelled for failure to file the affidavit of use no longer makes the former registrant the presumptive owner

questions.prompt: Under Section 123.1(e) of the Intellectual Property Code, as quoted in Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, which mark cannot be registered by another in the Philippines?

choices.A: A mark that is well-known only in the country where it was first used.
choices.B: Any mark that has been used abroad for more than one year.
choices.C: A mark considered by the competent authority of the Philippines to be well-known internationally and in the Philippines, whether or not it is registered here.
choices.D: A mark that has been registered in at least one foreign country.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court said that Section 123.1(e) categorically provides that "a mark which is considered by the competent authority of the Philippines to be well-known internationally and in the Philippines, whether or not it is registered here," cannot be registered by another in the Philippines. It does not require that the well-known mark be used in commerce in the Philippines, only that it be well-known in the Philippines. A is wrong because the mark must be well-known internationally and in the Philippines. B and D are wrong because use or registration abroad for a given time or in a single country is not the test; they are only some of the criteria that may be considered under Rule 102 in determining whether a mark is well-known.

questions.prompt: A foreign university has never registered its name as a trade name in the Philippines. According to Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, what protection does its trade name have here, given that its country and the Philippines are both parties to the Paris Convention?

choices.A: None, because only registered trade names are protected.
choices.B: Protection only after it has operated a campus in the Philippines.
choices.C: Protection only if the name is also registered as a trademark in the Philippines.
choices.D: Protection without the obligation of filing or registration, so that no one in the Philippines may use the name without its consent.

questions.explanation: D is correct. So under Philippine law the trade name of a national of a Paris Convention state is protected without filing or registration, and no educational entity in the Philippines can use the trade name "Harvard" without the university's consent. A and C are wrong because registration in the Philippines is not required. B is wrong because operating locally is not required.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company registers the word LOTUS, the name of a flower, as its brand for tire repair kits. A rival argues that the word is a common word of generic nature, so no one may appropriate it as a mark. Is the rival right? Explain, based on Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. What the law prohibits is not a mark with a generic meaning, but a mark that consists exclusively of signs that are generic for the goods or services it identifies. A flower name that does not identify tire repair kits can be appropriated as a mark.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 123 of the Intellectual Property Code prohibits the registration of a trademark that consists exclusively of signs that are generic for the goods or services that they seek to identify. So what is prohibited is not having a generic mark but having such a generic mark be identifiable to the good or service. Words that are generic or merely descriptive of an article, like "pale pilsen" for beer, cannot be appropriated by any one manufacturer because they belong to the public domain (Asia Brewery, Inc. v. Court of Appeals).
suggestedAnswer.application: LOTUS has a generic meaning as the name of a flower, but it does not identify or describe tire repair kits, and the kits cannot be identified with the flower. This is like SAKURA, the Japanese flowering cherry, for DVD and VCD players, in Kensonic: unlike "pale pilsen" in Asia Brewery, which described the beer itself, the word did not identify the goods. The word is therefore not generic for the goods and can be appropriated.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The rival is wrong. LOTUS can be appropriated as a mark for tire repair kits.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A maker of televisions and DVD players owns a registered mark. A different company later applies to register the same mark for washing machines and refrigerators. The first company opposes, arguing that it may one day make home appliances and that the mark should be protected for its normal potential expansion. Should the opposition succeed? Explain how a court decides whether goods are related, based on Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The prohibition against registering a confusingly similar mark extends only to goods that are related to the registered goods, not to goods that the owner might produce in the future. Whether goods are related is decided by looking at several factors, and on those factors home appliances are not related to audio-video goods.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The prohibition under Section 123 of the Intellectual Property Code extends to goods that are related to the registered goods, not to goods that the registrant may produce in the future; otherwise the right to a mark would depend on mere possibilities and conjectures. Non-competing goods are related if they are so related that it can reasonably be assumed that they originate from one manufacturer, so that confusion of business can arise from similar marks. If the goods are entirely unrelated, no common source can be assumed and there is no confusion of business. In Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery, the factors include the business to which the goods belong, the class of product, the nature and cost of the articles, their descriptive properties and essential characteristics, their purpose, whether they are bought for immediate consumption, the fields of manufacture, the conditions under which they are usually purchased, and the channels of trade.
suggestedAnswer.application: The first company's argument rests on what it may produce in the future, which is only a possibility and is not a basis for blocking registration. On the factors, washing machines and refrigerators differ from televisions and DVD players in class, descriptive attributes, purpose and conditions of sale, so it cannot reasonably be assumed that they originate from the same manufacturer. In Kensonic, the Court reached the same result for Uni-Line's Class 7 and 11 goods (home appliances) against Kensonic's audio-video goods.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The opposition should fail, because the goods are not related and the possibility of future expansion cannot be the basis of the prohibition.

A right to a trademark should not depend on mere possibilities and conjectures
Non-competing goods are related if it can reasonably be assumed that they come from one manufacturer, so that confusion of business may arise
Mighty Corporation factors: business, class, nature and cost, descriptive properties, purpose, fields of manufacture, conditions of purchase, channels of trade
Home appliances (Class 7 and Class 11) were unrelated to audio-video goods (Class 9) because of their differences in class, descriptive attributes, purposes and conditions

To allow the expansion of coverage is to prevent future registrants of goods from securing a trademark on the basis of mere possibilities and conjectures that may or may not occur at all. Surely, the right to a trademark should not be made to depend on mere possibilities and conjectures. … Non-competing goods may be those which, though they are not in actual competition, are so related to each other that it can reasonably be assumed that they originate from one manufacturer, in which case, confusion of business can arise out of the use of similar marks. They may also be those which, being entirely unrelated, cannot be assumed to have a common source; hence, there is no confusion of business, even though similar marks are used. … An examination of the foregoing factors reveals that the goods of Uni-Line were not related to the goods of Kensonic by virtue of their differences in class, the descriptive attributes, the purposes and the conditions of the goods.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company owns a registered mark for televisions and DVD players, which are in Class 9 of the Nice Classification. A competitor applies to register a nearly identical mark for voltage regulators and fuses, which are also in Class 9. The first company argues that all goods in Class 9 are related, so the application should be refused. Is the argument correct? Explain, based on Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Goods are not related merely because they belong to the same class. Class 9 can be sub-classified, and televisions and DVD players are in a different sub-class and are final products, unlike voltage regulators and fuses.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The mere fact that goods belong to the same class does not necessarily mean that they are related. Classification under the Nice Classification is only part of the factors to be considered in determining whether goods are related, and the factors of Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery must be considered (Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.). Class 9 can be sub-categorized into five classifications: (1) apparatus and instruments for scientific or research purposes, (2) information technology and audiovisual equipment, (3) apparatus and devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity, (4) optical apparatus and instruments, and (5) safety equipment.
suggestedAnswer.application: Televisions and DVD players belong to the information technology and audiovisual equipment sub-class. Voltage regulators and fuses pertain to the sub-class of apparatus and devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity. The first company's goods are also final products, while the applicant's Class 9 goods are spare parts. Given these distinctions, the goods are unrelated even though both are in Class 9, as the Court held for Uni-Line's voltage regulators, portable generators, switch breakers and fuses.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The argument is not correct. Same class does not make the goods related, and the application for the unrelated goods may be allowed.

keyPoints: Belonging to the same class does not necessarily mean that goods are related
The Nice classification is only one of many factors, and the factors of Mighty Corporation must be considered
Class 9 has five sub-classifications, such as audiovisual equipment and devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity
Final products and spare parts are different
Voltage regulators, portable generators, switch breakers and fuses were unrelated to televisions and DVD players

source.part: Part III (the goods of Kensonic were also unrelated to the goods of Uni-Line although both belonged to Class 9)
source.excerpt: In Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics, Co., Inc., the Court has opined that the mere fact that goods belonged to the same class does not necessarily mean that they are related; and that the factors listed in Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery should be taken into consideration … It bears to stress at this point that the list of products included in Class 9 can be sub-categorized into five (5) classifications, namely: (1) apparatus and instruments for scientific or research purposes, (2) information technology and audiovisual equipment, (3) apparatus and devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity, (4) optical apparatus and instruments, and (5) safety equipment. … Based on the foregoing pronouncement in Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics, Co., Inc., there are other sub-classifications present even if the goods are classified under Class 09. For one, Kensonic's goods belonged to the information technology and audiovisual equipment subclass, but Uni-Line's goods pertained to the apparatus and devices for controlling the distribution of electricity sub-class. Also, the Class 09 goods of Kensonic were final products but Uni-Line's Class 09 products were spare parts. In view of these distinctions, the Court agrees with Uni-Line that its Class 09 goods were unrelated to the Class 09 goods of Kensonic.

questions.prompt: A party argues that a trademark cannot be appropriated because the word is "not copyrightable". According to Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc., why is the argument misplaced?

choices.A: Because a mark is a visible sign that distinguishes the goods or services of an enterprise, while a copyright is a statutory right over literary or artistic works; a mark is not an artistic or literary work.
choices.B: Because every word that can be registered as a mark is automatically protected by copyright.
choices.C: Because copyright and trademark protection are the same right under different names.
choices.D: Because copyright can be acquired only by registration, while a mark cannot be registered.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court noted that the controversy revolved around a mark, not a copyright, and that the distinction is significant. A mark is any visible sign capable of distinguishing the goods (trademark) or services (service mark) of an enterprise, while a copyright is the right to literary property recognized by law, an intangible right granted by statute to the author or originator of literary or artistic productions for a specific period. The SAKURA mark is not an artistic or literary work but a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from those of another. B and C are wrong because the two rights are different. D is wrong because marks can be registered, which is the point of the case.

source.caseTitle: Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc. (Phil.)
source.part: Part I (The SAKURA mark can be appropriated)
source.excerpt: To be noted is that the controversy revolves around the SAKURA mark which is not a copyright. The distinction is significant. A mark is any visible sign capable of distinguishing the goods (trademark) or services (service mark) of an enterprise, and includes a stamped or marked container of goods. In contrast, a copyright is the right to literary property as recognized and sanctioned by positive law; it is an intangible, incorporeal right granted by statute to the author or originator of certain literary or artistic productions, whereby he or she is invested, for a specific period, with the sole and exclusive privilege of multiplying copies of the same and publishing and selling them. Obviously, the SAKURA mark is not an artistic or literary work but a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from those of another.

questions.prompt: In a petition for review on certiorari, a party asks the Supreme Court to re-examine whether its opponent owns a mark through prior use, a point already decided by the intellectual property office and affirmed by the Court of Appeals. According to Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc., how should the Court treat the request?

choices.A: It re-weighs the evidence, because trademark ownership is always a question of law.
choices.B: It sends the question back to the Bureau of Legal Affairs for a new hearing.
choices.C: It accepts the party's version of the facts without examination.
choices.D: It declines, because a petition for review on certiorari is limited to questions of law, the Court is not a trier of facts, and findings of the quasi-judicial body affirmed by the Court of Appeals are binding, subject to exceptions that the petitioner has the burden of showing.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court said that reviewing Kensonic's ownership would entail examining facts already settled by the lower tribunals, and that it cannot act on a factual matter in an appeal under Rule 45, which is limited to questions of law. It reminded that the Court is not a trier of facts, so the factual findings of a quasi-judicial body like the IPO, especially when affirmed by the Court of Appeals, are binding on the Court. There are exceptions, but Uni-Line did not discharge its burden to show that its request came within any of them. A is wrong because ownership by use here was a factual finding. B and C are not what the Court did. Watch for: the Court treated Kensonic's prior use since 1994 as making it the owner; in a later decision, Zuneca v. Natrapharm (2020), the Court held that under the Intellectual Property Code ownership is acquired through registration, so check how the rule applies to a mark first used or registered after the Code took effect.

source.caseTitle: Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc. (Phil.)
source.part: Part I (ownership and the limits of review under Rule 45)
source.excerpt: Kensonic's prior use of the mark since 1994 made it the owner of the mark, and its ownership cannot anymore be challenged at this stage of the proceedings. Seeking the review of Kensonic's ownership would entail the examination of facts already settled by the lower tribunals. … It is timely to remind, too, that the Court is not a trier of facts. Hence, the factual findings of the quasi-judicial body like the IPO, especially when affirmed by the CA, are binding on the Court. Jurisprudence has laid down certain exceptions to the rule of bindingness, but, alas, Uni-Line did not discharge its burden to show how its urging for a review of the factual findings came within any of the exceptions.

According to Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc., how far does the prohibition under Section 123 of the Intellectual Property Code extend?

choices.A: To all goods in the same market, whether or not they are related to the registered goods.
choices.B: To any goods the registrant says it intends to produce in the future.
choices.C: To goods that the registrant may produce in the next ten years.
choices.D: To goods that are related to the registered goods, not to goods that the registrant may produce in the future.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court held that the prohibition under Section 123 extends to goods related to the registered goods, not to goods that the registrant may produce in the future. To allow the expansion of coverage would prevent future registrants of goods from securing a trademark on the basis of mere possibilities and conjectures that may or may not occur at all, and the right to a trademark should not be made to depend on such possibilities. A is wrong because relatedness, not mere presence in the same market, is the test. B and C are wrong because future production is exactly what the Court said is not covered. Watch for: the decision in Dermaline (2010) spoke of protection for the normal potential expansion of the registered owner's business; the Court in this case limited the prohibition to related goods, so check how the two apply.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc. (applying Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery), which of the following is one of the factors that decide whether goods are related?

choices.A: The nationality of the founders of each company.
choices.B: The channels of trade through which the goods flow, and how they are distributed, marketed, displayed and sold.
choices.C: The number of employees of each company.
choices.D: The date on which each company was incorporated.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The factors the Court listed include the business and its location to which the goods belong; the class of product; the quality, quantity or size of the product, including the package; the nature and cost of the articles; their descriptive properties, physical attributes or essential characteristics; the purpose of the goods; whether the article is bought for immediate consumption, that is, a day-to-day household item; the fields of manufacture; the conditions under which the article is usually purchased; and the channels of trade through which the goods flow, how they are distributed, marketed, displayed and sold. A, C and D describe the companies and not the goods, and are not among the factors.

source.caseTitle: Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc. (Phil.)
source.part: Part II (the factors for deciding whether goods are related)
source.excerpt: In resolving whether goods are related, several factors come into play: (a) the business (and its location) to which the goods belong (b) the class of product to which the goods belong (c) the product's quality, quantity, or size, including the nature of the package, wrapper or container (d) the nature and cost of the articles (e) the descriptive properties, physical attributes or essential characteristics with reference to their form, composition, texture or quality (f) the purpose of the goods (g) whether the article is bought for immediate consumption, that is, day-to-day household items (h) the fields of manufacture (i) the conditions under which the article is usually purchased and (j) the channels of trade through which the goods flow, how they are distributed, marketed, displayed and sold.

questions.prompt: In the end, what did the Court decide in Kensonic, Inc. v. Uni-Line Multi-Resources, Inc. about the registration of the SAKURA mark by Uni-Line for voltage regulators, portable generators, switch breakers and fuses?

choices.B: It cancelled the registration of all of Uni-Line's goods in every class.
choices.C: It transferred the registration to Kensonic.
choices.D: It allowed Uni-Line to register SAKURA for those goods, by partially reinstating the Court of Appeals' first decision, and ordered Kensonic to pay the costs.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company sues a competitor in 1993 for infringing its trademark. The trial court decides the case in 1998 and holds the competitor liable under the old Trademark Law and also under a new Intellectual Property Code that took effect on January 1, 1998. The Court of Appeals affirms. Was it correct to apply the new Code? Which law governs, and what if the old Trademark Law conflicts with the Paris Convention? Explain, based on Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The new Code was applied retroactively, which was an error. The complaint is governed by the law in force when it was filed, the Trademark Law and the Paris Convention, and if the two conflict, the municipal Trademark Law prevails.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The validity and obligatory force of a law proceed from its promulgation, and a law that is not yet effective cannot be considered as known by the populace. A new state of the law ought to affect the future, not the past, and any doubt must be resolved against the retroactive operation of laws, whether they are original enactments, amendments or repeals. The Intellectual Property Code was approved on June 6, 1997, and Section 241 provided that it was to take effect on January 1, 1998, with no provision for retroactive application. In case of domestic legal disputes on conflicting provisions between the Paris Convention (an international agreement) and the Trademark Law (a municipal law), the latter prevails.
suggestedAnswer.application: The complaint was filed in 1993, about five years before the Code took effect, and the Code has no clause giving it retroactive effect. So the trial court and the Court of Appeals should have limited their consideration of the case to the Trademark Law and the Paris Convention, the laws in force when the complaint was filed. Where the Trademark Law and the Paris Convention conflict, the Trademark Law governs.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The courts erred in retroactively applying the Code; the old Trademark Law and the Paris Convention (with the Trademark Law prevailing in a conflict) govern.

keyPoints: A law has no force until it takes effect; the new Code took effect on January 1, 1998 (Section 241)
Laws are not applied retroactively, and doubts are resolved against retroactive operation
The case should be decided under the laws in force when the complaint was filed (the Trademark Law and the Paris Convention)
In a conflict between the Paris Convention and the Trademark Law, the municipal law prevails

source.caseTitle: Mighty Corporation and La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. v. E. & J. Gallo Winery and The Andresons Group, Inc.
source.part: The Trademark Law and the Paris Convention are the applicable laws, not the Intellectual Property Code; the Paris Convention and the Trademark Law
source.excerpt: We therefore hold that the courts a quo erred in retroactively applying the IP Code in this case. … Nova constitutio futuris formam imponere debet non praeteritis. A new state of the law ought to affect the future, not the past. Any doubt must generally be resolved against the retroactive operation of laws, whether these are original enactments, amendments or repeals. … The IP Code, repealing the Trademark Law, was approved on June 6, 1997. Section 241 thereof expressly decreed that it was to take effect only on January 1, 1998, without any provision for retroactive application. Thus, the Makati RTC and the CA should have limited the consideration of the present case within the parameters of the Trademark Law and the Paris Convention, the laws in force at the time of the filing of the complaint. … Following universal acquiescence and comity, in case of domestic legal disputes on any conflicting provisions between the Paris Convention (which is an international agreement) and the Trademark law (which is a municipal law) the latter will prevail.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A person who has no registered mark sells goods in packaging made to look like a competitor's well-known goods, so that buyers are led to believe that they are the competitor's, and does so deliberately. Another person uses a registered mark of a competitor on its own goods without consent, but honestly and without any intent to deceive. How do trademark infringement and unfair competition differ, and which of the two persons may be liable for what? Explain, based on Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The first person is liable for unfair competition, which does not need a registered mark but needs fraudulent intent and passing off. The second may be liable for trademark infringement, which needs a registered mark and the unauthorized use of it, but not fraudulent intent, provided the other elements are present.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The laws on trademark infringement and unfair competition share a common root: a person shall not be permitted to misrepresent his goods or business as the goods or business of another. Unfair competition is broader and more inclusive; infringement is narrower but recognizes a more exclusive right from adoption and registration of the mark. Even a person who fails to establish an exclusive right to a trademark may still obtain relief for a competitor's unfairness or fraud, and conduct is unfair competition if the effect is to pass off on the public the goods of one man as those of another. As distinguished in Del Monte: (1) infringement is the unauthorized use of a trademark, while unfair competition is the passing off of one's goods as those of another; (2) in infringement fraudulent intent is unnecessary, while in unfair competition it is essential; and (3) in infringement prior registration of the trademark is a prerequisite, while in unfair competition registration is not necessary. The universal test question for unfair competition is whether the public is likely to be deceived.
suggestedAnswer.application: The first person has no registered mark, and so cannot be accused of infringement by it, but its deliberate packaging that leads buyers to think that the goods are the competitor's is passing off with fraudulent intent, which is unfair competition. The second person used a registered mark without consent, so, if the other elements of infringement exist (including use on identical or similar goods and likelihood of confusion), its good faith does not excuse infringement because fraudulent intent is unnecessary. But it would not be liable for unfair competition without proof of bad faith or an attempt to pass off.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The first person is liable for unfair competition; the second may be liable for infringement but not for unfair competition.

keyPoints: Common root: no one may misrepresent his goods or business as those of another
Infringement is the unauthorized use of a trademark; unfair competition is passing off one's goods as those of another
Fraudulent intent is unnecessary in infringement but essential in unfair competition
Prior registration is a prerequisite in infringement but not in unfair competition
Unfair competition is broader and more inclusive; the test is whether the public is likely to be deceived

source.caseTitle: Mighty Corporation and La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. v. E. & J. Gallo Winery and The Andresons Group, Inc.
source.part: Distinctions between trademark infringement and unfair competition; Petitioners are also not liable for unfair competition
source.excerpt: Although the laws on trademark infringement and unfair competition have a common conception at their root, that is, a person shall not be permitted to misrepresent his goods or his business as the goods or business of another, the law on unfair competition is broader and more inclusive than the law on trademark infringement. … Hence, even if one fails to establish his exclusive property right to a trademark, he may still obtain relief on the ground of his competitor’s unfairness or fraud. Conduct constitutes unfair competition if the effect is to pass off on the public the goods of one man as the goods of another. … (1) Infringement of trademark is the unauthorized use of a trademark, whereas unfair competition is the passing off of one's goods as those of another. (2) In infringement of trademark fraudulent intent is unnecessary, whereas in unfair competition fraudulent intent is essential. (3) In infringement of trademark the prior registration of the trademark is a prerequisite to the action, whereas in unfair competition registration is not necessary. … The universal test question is whether the public is likely to be deceived.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A maker of imported wine, whose mark is registered for wine only, sues a local cigarette maker that uses the same word as a cigarette brand. The courts below hold that wine and cigarettes are related goods because both are forms of vice, harmful in excess and used for pleasure, and because both are sold in the same section of supermarkets. Are wine and cigarettes related goods? Explain, based on Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The two reasons are insufficient and arbitrary. Wine and cigarettes are not identical, similar, competing or related goods, so use of the same word as a mark on both is not likely to cause confusion.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under the modern concept of related goods, trademark infringement occurs when goods are so related that the public may be, or is actually, deceived into believing that they come from the same maker. Non-competing goods are related if it can reasonably be assumed that they come from one manufacturer; if they are entirely unrelated, there is no confusion of business even if similar marks are used. No single factor is preeminent: the court weighs the factors, including the class and nature of the goods, their cost, descriptive properties, purpose, conditions of purchase and channels of trade. Product classification alone is not decisive, and the mere fact that one person has adopted and used a mark for his goods does not prevent others from using it on articles of a different description. Tobacco and alcohol products may be considered related only in special circumstances, which exist only if a famous mark is involved and there is a demonstrated intent to capitalize on it.
suggestedAnswer.application: Anything, not only wine and cigarettes, can be used for pleasure and relaxation and can be harmful in excess, and supermarkets sell an infinite variety of unrelated products, so being sold in one store under one roof does not make buyers likely to be confused about the source. Wine is bottled and drunk and cigarettes are packed and smoked, so their properties differ greatly. Cigarettes are cheap and sold to low-income buyers through vendors and sari-sari stores, while the wine is expensive, imported and sold in hotels, bars and high-end stores, so the price difference shows different buyers and different channels of trade. There was no famous mark and no proven intent to capitalize on it, so the special circumstances for tobacco and alcohol do not exist.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Wine and cigarettes are non-competing and unrelated goods, and there is no likelihood of confusion.

keyPoints: Goods are related when the public may be deceived into thinking that they come from the same maker
Being forms of vice or pleasure, or being sold in the same supermarket section, is not enough
Different descriptive properties, price, buyers and channels of trade show that goods are unrelated
No single factor is decisive; the court weighs all of them
Tobacco and alcohol are related only in special circumstances: a famous mark and a demonstrated intent to capitalize on it

source.caseTitle: Mighty Corporation and La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. v. E. & J. Gallo Winery and The Andresons Group, Inc.
source.part: Wines and cigarettes are not identical, similar, competing or related goods
source.excerpt: We find these premises patently insufficient and too arbitrary to support the legal conclusion that wines and cigarettes are related products within the contemplation of the Trademark Law and the Paris Convention. … Accordingly, the U.S. patent office and courts have consistently held that the mere fact that goods are sold in one store under the same roof does not automatically mean that buyers are likely to be confused as to the goods’ respective sources, connections or sponsorships. The fact that different products are available in the same store is an insufficient standard, in and of itself, to warrant a finding of likelihood of confusion. … GALLO cigarettes are inexpensive items while GALLO wines are not. GALLO wines are patronized by middle-to-high-income earners while GALLO cigarettes appeal only to simple folks like farmers, fishermen, laborers and other low-income workers. Indeed, the big price difference of these two products is an important factor in proving that they are in fact unrelated and that they travel in different channels of trade. … In short, tobacco and alcohol products may be considered related only in cases involving special circumstances which exist only if a famous mark is involved and there is a demonstrated intent to capitalize on it. Both of these are absent in the present case.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under Sections 2, 2-A, 9-A, 20 and 22 of the old Trademark Law, as the Court summarized them in Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery, which of the following is an element of trademark infringement?

choices.A: That the infringer acted with fraudulent intent.
choices.B: That the trademark owner is a foreign corporation doing business in the Philippines.
choices.C: That the trademark is actually used in commerce in the Philippines and registered in the principal register of the Philippine Patent Office.
choices.D: That the infringer's goods are of lower quality than the owner's goods.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court listed the elements of infringement under the Trademark Law: (a) a trademark actually used in commerce in the Philippines and registered in the principal register of the Philippine Patent Office; (b) is used by another person in connection with the sale, offering for sale or advertising of goods, business or services in a way likely to cause confusion, mistake or deception, or is reproduced or colorably imitated and applied to labels, packages or advertisements; (c) the trademark is used for identical or similar goods; and (d) the act is done without the consent of the trademark registrant or assignee. A is wrong because fraudulent intent is unnecessary in infringement but essential in unfair competition. B and D are not elements. Watch for: this is the rule under the old Trademark Law applied in the decision; the Intellectual Property Code now governs, so check its current text.

source.caseTitle: Mighty Corporation and La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. v. E. & J. Gallo Winery and The Andresons Group, Inc.
source.part: Pertinent provisions on trademark infringement under the Paris Convention and the Trademark Law
source.excerpt: Under Sections 2, 2-A, 9-A, 20 and 22 of the Trademark Law therefore, the following constitute the elements of trademark infringement: (a) a trademark actually used in commerce in the Philippines and registered in the principal register of the Philippine Patent Office … (c) the trademark is used for identical or similar goods, and (d) such act is done without the consent of the trademark registrant or assignee.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the old Trademark Law, a foreign company registered a mark for one product in 1971 but first sold goods under it in the Philippines only in 1974 (in U.S. military facilities) and 1979 (elsewhere). A local company had used the same word for a different product since 1973. According to Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery, what was the effect of the foreign company's late use?

choices.A: None; registration alone gives an exclusive right against everyone from the date of registration.
choices.B: The foreign company never enjoyed an exclusive right to use the mark against the local company, because actual commercial use in the Philippines was an essential prerequisite and the local company's use came earlier.
choices.C: The local company's use was void because it was not registered.
choices.D: The foreign company's registration was automatically cancelled.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court gave utmost importance to the actual commercial use of a trademark in the Philippines before registration under Sections 2 and 2-A of the Trademark Law, notwithstanding the Paris Convention. Gallo Winery admitted that its wine was first sold in the Philippines only in 1974 and 1979, while Tobacco Industries, the predecessor of Mighty, had used GALLO for cigarettes since 1973, supported by BIR authorizations and a sworn statement. So the Court ruled that Gallo Winery never enjoyed the exclusive right to use its mark to the prejudice of Tobacco Industries and its successors, under either the Trademark Law or the Paris Convention. A is wrong because registration is only prima facie evidence and is not conclusive. C and D are not what the Court said. Watch for: this reflects the use-based rule of the old Trademark Law; in Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm (2020) the Court held that under the Intellectual Property Code ownership of a mark is acquired through registration, so check which law applies.

source.caseTitle: Mighty Corporation and La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. v. E. & J. Gallo Winery and The Andresons Group, Inc.
source.part: The actual commercial use in the Philippines of the GALLO cigarette trademark preceded that of the GALLO wine trademark
source.excerpt: By respondents’ own judicial admission, the GALLO wine trademark was registered in the Philippines in November 1971 but the wine itself was first marketed and sold in the country only in 1974 and only within the former U.S. military facilities, and outside thereof, only in 1979. … On the other hand, by testimonial evidence supported by the BIR authorization letters, forms and manufacturer’s sworn statement, it appears that petitioners and its predecessor-in-interest, Tobacco Industries, have indeed been using and selling GALLO cigarettes in the Philippines since 1973 or before July 9, 1981. … we rule that, on this account, respondents never enjoyed the exclusive right to use the GALLO wine trademark to the prejudice of Tobacco Industries and its successors-in-interest, herein petitioners, either under the Trademark Law or the Paris Convention.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A trademark's registration certificate states that it covers one product only. According to Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery, applying Section 20 of the old Trademark Law, how far does the registrant's exclusive right to use the mark extend?

choices.A: Only to the product indicated in the registration certificate, subject to the rule on identical or similar goods and related goods.
choices.B: To every product the registrant may ever decide to sell.
choices.C: To all goods of any kind, because the mark is registered.
choices.D: To every product sold in the same stores as the registered product.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court noted that the registration certificates expressly state that they cover wines only, without evidence that Gallo Winery expanded or intended to expand to cigarettes. By strict application of Section 20 of the Trademark Law, the exclusive right to use GALLO should be limited to wines, the only product indicated in the certificates. The Court quoted the principle in Faberge that the certificate confers the exclusive right to use the symbol only for the goods specified in it, and that an omnibus registration of all goods the applicant can conceive is not contemplated by the Trademark Law. The Court then separately considered whether the other goods were identical, similar or related (the modern concept of related goods). B, C and D describe the omnibus registration the Court rejected. Watch for: this is the rule of the old Trademark Law applied in the decision; check the current law for registrations under the Intellectual Property Code.

source.caseTitle: Mighty Corporation and La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. v. E. & J. Gallo Winery and The Andresons Group, Inc.
source.part: Respondents' GALLO trademark registration is limited to wines only
source.excerpt: We also note that the GALLO trademark registration certificates in the Philippines and in other countries expressly state that they cover wines only, without any evidence or indication that registrant Gallo Winery expanded or intended to expand its business to cigarettes. Thus, by strict application of Section 20 of the Trademark Law, Gallo Winery’s exclusive right to use the GALLO trademark should be limited to wines, the only product indicated in its registration certificates.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery, in determining the likelihood of confusion the court considers the resemblance of the marks, the similarity of the goods and the likely effect on the purchaser. What is the fourth consideration?

choices.A: The nationality of the parties.
choices.B: The number of years each party has been in business.
choices.C: The amount of money each party spent on advertising.
choices.D: The registrant's express or implied consent and other fair and equitable considerations.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court said that in determining the likelihood of confusion it must consider [a] the resemblance between the trademarks; [b] the similarity of the goods to which the trademarks are attached; [c] the likely effect on the purchaser; and [d] the registrant's express or implied consent and other fair and equitable considerations. On the last point, the Court noted that respondents took almost twenty years to learn of GALLO cigarettes and sue, and their delay, together with implied consent, acquiescence or negligence, led it to hold that equity, justice and fairness favored the cigarette makers. A, B and C are not among the considerations the Court listed.

source.caseTitle: Mighty Corporation and La Campana Fabrica de Tabaco, Inc. v. E. & J. Gallo Winery and The Andresons Group, Inc.
source.part: No likelihood of confusion, mistake or deceit; consent of the registrant and other fair, just and equitable considerations
source.excerpt: In determining the likelihood of confusion, the Court must consider: [a] the resemblance between the trademarks; [b] the similarity of the goods to which the trademarks are attached; [c] the likely effect on the purchaser and [d] the registrant’s express or implied consent and other fair and equitable considerations. … It took respondents almost 20 years to know about the existence of GALLO cigarettes and sue petitioners for trademark infringement. Given, on one hand, the long period of time that petitioners were engaged in the manufacture, marketing, distribution and sale of GALLO cigarettes and, on the other, respondents’ delay in enforcing their rights (not to mention implied consent, acquiescence or negligence) we hold that equity, justice and fairness require us to rule in favor of petitioners.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A foreign company claims that its mark is well known and protected under Article 6bis of the Paris Convention against a local company that uses the same word on a different kind of goods. According to Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery (applying the guidelines of the Minister of Trade quoted in Canon), what must be true of the mark to be protected as well-known?

choices.A: It must have been registered in at least ten countries.
choices.B: It must be used on the same or similar kinds of goods as the local company's goods.
choices.C: It must be a mark that is older than the local company.
choices.D: It must be a fanciful mark rather than a family name.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court held that GALLO could not be considered a well-known mark within the contemplation and protection of the Paris Convention in this case because wines and cigarettes are not identical or similar goods. It quoted the guidelines issued by the Minister of Trade and Industry to implement Article 6bis: (a) the mark must be internationally known; (b) the subject of the right must be a trademark, not a patent or copyright or anything else; (c) the mark must be for use in the same or similar kinds of goods; and (d) the person claiming must be the owner of the mark. The foreign company failed the third condition. A, C and D are not conditions in the guidelines. Watch for: the decision applied the 1983 guidelines under the Paris Convention; the later decision in Fredco v. Harvard (2011) also discusses well-known marks, so check how the two apply.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: An intellectual property office rejects an application to register a mark, saying: "The mark is identical to a registered mark, and both are used on goods in the same class of the Nice Classification. On this point alone, the application should be denied." Is this reasoning correct? Explain, based on Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Identity of the marks and uniformity of classification do not, by themselves, decide the matter. What matters is whether the goods themselves are similar or related, not the classification in which they were placed.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Mere uniformity in categorization does not automatically preclude the registration of what appears to be an identical mark, and in a long line of cases the Court has held that this circumstance does not necessarily result in trademark infringement. Whether the goods fall under the same categories of the Nice Classification is not the sole and decisive factor. Emphasis should be on the similarity of the products involved and not on the arbitrary classification or general description of their properties or characteristics. The mere fact that one person has adopted and used a trademark on his goods does not, without more, prevent the adoption and use of the same trademark by others on unrelated articles of a different kind. Examples in the cases cited include LOTUS for soy sauce despite a prior LOTUS for edible oil in the same class, CAMIA for ham despite a prior CAMIA for lard, butter and soap, and HICKOK for shoes despite a prior HICKOK for handkerchiefs, briefs, belts and wallets.
suggestedAnswer.application: The office decided the case on only two points, identity of the marks and the same class, and so it ignored the question that matters: whether the applicant's goods and the registered goods are similar or related. Without an examination of the goods themselves, the rejection cannot stand on that reasoning alone. The identical-mark-and-same-class argument was called specious by the Court.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The reasoning is not correct. The application cannot be denied on the sole ground of an identical mark in the same class; the court must examine whether the goods are actually related.

keyPoints: Uniformity in categorization does not automatically preclude the registration of an identical mark
The Nice Classification of goods is not the sole and decisive factor
Emphasis should be on the similarity of the products and not on an arbitrary classification
The prior use of a mark on one kind of goods does not, without more, prevent others from using it on unrelated articles
Examples: LOTUS, CAMIA and HICKOK

source.caseTitle: Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.
source.part: Identical marks may be registered for products from the same classification
source.excerpt: On this point alone, Respondent-Applicant’s application should already be denied. The argument is specious. … But mere uniformity in categorization, by itself, does not automatically preclude the registration of what appears to be an identical mark, if that be the case. In fact, this Court, in a long line of cases, has held that such circumstance does not necessarily result in any trademark infringement. … Verily, whether or not the products covered by the trademark sought to be registered by Taiwan Kolin, on the one hand, and those covered by the prior issued certificate of registration in favor of Kolin Electronics, on the other, fall under the same categories in the NCL is not the sole and decisive factor in determining a possible violation of Kolin Electronics’ intellectual property right should petitioner’s application be granted. It is hornbook doctrine, as held in the above-cited cases, that emphasis should be on the similarity of the products involved and not on the arbitrary classification or general description of their properties or characteristics. The mere fact that one person has adopted and used a trademark on his goods would not, without more, prevent the adoption and use of the same trademark by others on unrelated articles of a different kind.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company that makes televisions and DVD players applies to register a mark that is identical to a mark registered by another company for voltage regulators, converters and stereo boosters. The opponent argues that all of these are electronic products that plug into sockets, so they are related goods. The applicant answers that its goods are home appliances that are sold wholesale to accredited dealers, while the opponent's goods are sold in electrical and hardware stores. Are the goods related? Explain, based on Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. It is not enough that all of the goods are electronic products in the same class. The goods must be tested against several factors, and on those factors the applicant's home appliances and the opponent's power and audio accessories are not related.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A certificate of registration gives the owner the exclusive right to sue those who adopt a similar mark for the goods or services in the certificate and also for those that are related to them. Under Mighty Corporation v. E. & J. Gallo Winery, relatedness is tested against several factors, including the business to which the goods belong, the class of product, the nature and cost of the articles, their descriptive properties, their purpose, the fields of manufacture, the conditions under which they are purchased, and the channels of trade through which they flow. Classification under the Nice Classification is only part of the factors, and stating that the goods are electronic products in Class 9 accounts for only one of many considerations. Class 9 can be sub-categorized into five classifications, among them information technology and audiovisual equipment, and apparatus and devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity.
suggestedAnswer.application: The applicant's televisions and DVD players are audiovisual equipment sold as home appliances, with a function and purpose different from the opponent's voltage regulators, converters and boosters, which are devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity. They are also sold through different channels: wholesale to accredited dealers, as against electrical and hardware stores. In this digital age, when electronic products have diversified greatly, it is difficult to say that all devices that plug into sockets are necessarily related goods. So it is wrong to conclude that all electronic products are related, or that the registration of one electronic product precludes the registration of a similar mark for another.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The goods are unrelated, and the opposition based on relatedness fails.

keyPoints: The registration protects against similar marks on the goods specified and on related goods
Relatedness is tested against the Mighty Corporation factors, not only classification
Stating that the goods are electronic products in Class 9 is only one consideration
Class 9 has sub-classifications, such as audiovisual equipment and devices for controlling the distribution and use of electricity
Different function and purpose and different channels of trade point to unrelated goods
Not all devices that plug into sockets are necessarily related goods

source.caseTitle: Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.
source.part: The products covered by petitioner's application and respondent's registration are unrelated
source.excerpt: A certificate of trademark registration confers upon the trademark owner the exclusive right to sue those who have adopted a similar mark not only in connection with the goods or services specified in the certificate, but also with those that are related thereto. … As mentioned, the classification of the products under the NCL is merely part and parcel of the factors to be considered in ascertaining whether the goods are related. It is not sufficient to state that the goods involved herein are electronic products under Class 9 in order to establish relatedness between the goods, for this only accounts for one of many considerations enumerated in Mighty Corporation. In this case, credence is accorded to petitioner’s assertions that: a. Taiwan Kolin’s goods are classified as home appliances as opposed to Kolin Electronics’ goods which are power supply and audio equipment accessories; b. Taiwan Kolin’s television sets and DVD players perform distinct function and purpose from Kolin Electronics’ power supply and audio equipment; and c. Taiwan Kolin sells and distributes its various home appliance products on wholesale and to accredited dealers, whereas Kolin Electronics’ goods are sold and flow through electrical and hardware stores. … Clearly then, it was erroneous for respondent to assume over the CA to conclude that all electronic products are related and that the coverage of one electronic product necessarily precludes the registration of a similar mark over another.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Two marks use the same word in capital letters. One is black, italicized lettering, and the other is white lettering on a red background. They are used for relatively expensive electronic goods that are bought rarely and last for years. Is an ordinary buyer likely to be confused? Explain how the character of the buyer and the cost of the goods affect the test, based on Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The differences between the marks, even if subtle, are enough, and for relatively expensive, rarely bought goods the ordinary buyer is an ordinarily intelligent buyer who is more discerning, so confusion is less likely.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In trademark cases no rigid rules can be formulated; each case is decided on its merits with due regard to the goods involved and the usual purchaser's character and attitude, and precedents are to be applied only if specifically in point. The cost of the goods essentially determines the attitude of the purchaser: an ordinary buyer does not exercise as much prudence in buying an article for which he pays a few centavos as in buying a more valuable thing, and expensive and valuable items are normally bought after deliberate, comparative and analytical investigation. The "ordinary purchaser" is not the completely unwary consumer but the ordinarily intelligent buyer considering the type of product involved, one who is familiar with the article he seeks to buy.
suggestedAnswer.application: The marks are both the same word in upper case bold letters, but there are distinct visual and aural differences: one is italic and black, the other is white on a red background, and these differences, though they may appear minimal, are enough to distinguish one brand from the other. The goods are relatively luxury items, not ordinary consumable household items of minimal cost, and they have long useful lives so replacement purchases are infrequent and the price can exceed a month's minimum wage. The casual buyer will be cautious and discriminating and will mull over the purchase, so he is expected to be more discerning in choosing among electronic products.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: An ordinarily intelligent buyer is not likely to be confused, and the application is not likely to cause confusion or deception.

keyPoints: No rigid rules; each case is decided on its merits, and precedents apply only if specifically in point
The cost of the goods essentially determines how careful the purchaser is
Expensive and valuable items are bought after deliberate, comparative and analytical investigation
The ordinary purchaser is the ordinarily intelligent buyer for the type of product, not the completely unwary consumer
Subtle visual and aural differences (italic black v. white on red) can be enough to distinguish brands

source.caseTitle: Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.
source.part: The ordinarily intelligent buyer is not likely to be confused
source.excerpt: While both competing marks refer to the word "KOLIN" written in upper case letters and in bold font, the Court at once notes the distinct visual and aural differences between them: Kolin Electronics’ mark is italicized and colored black while that of Taiwan Kolin is white in pantone red color background. The differing features between the two, though they may appear minimal, are sufficient to distinguish one brand from the other. … These are not ordinary consumable household items, like catsup, soy sauce or soap which are of minimal cost. The products of the contending parties are relatively luxury items not easily considered affordable. Accordingly, the casual buyer is predisposed to be more cautious and discriminating in and would prefer to mull over his purchase. Confusion and deception, then, is less likely. … In light of these circumstances, it is then expected that the ordinary intelligent buyer would be more discerning when it comes to deciding which electronic product they are going to purchase, and it is this standard which this Court applies herein in determining the likelihood of confusion should petitioner’s application be granted.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A party in a trademark case cites many earlier decisions to show that the goods in its case are related. According to Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc., how should precedents on confusing similarity be used?

choices.A: They bind the court in every trademark case, whatever the facts.
choices.B: They should be disregarded, because trademark cases have no precedents.
choices.C: They are used only to decide the amount of damages.
choices.D: No rigid rules can be formulated; each case is decided on its merits, and precedents should be applied only if they are specifically in point.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court said that in ascertaining whether one trademark is confusingly similar to another, no rigid set of rules can plausibly be formulated, and each case must be decided on its merits with due regard to the goods or services involved and the usual purchaser's character and attitude. Precedent must be studied in the light of the facts of the particular case, so jurisprudential precedents should be applied only if they are specifically in point. The Court then distinguished the cases cited by the respondent (which involved common household items such as biscuits and milk, cosmetics, clothes and toilet articles) from the present case, which involved relatively expensive electronic goods. A and B are wrong because precedents are studied but applied only where in point. C has no basis in the decision.

source.caseTitle: Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.
source.part: The ordinarily intelligent buyer is not likely to be confused
source.excerpt: In trademark cases, particularly in ascertaining whether one trademark is confusingly similar to another, no rigid set rules can plausible be formulated. Each case must be decided on its merits, with due regard to the goods or services involved, the usual purchaser’s character and attitude, among others. In such cases, even more than in any other litigation, precedent must be studied in the light of the facts of a particular case. That is the reason why in trademark cases, jurisprudential precedents should be applied only to a case if they are specifically in point.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In deciding whether an application to register a mark would cause confusion, the Court in Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc. (quoting Emerald Garment) described the "ordinary purchaser". Who is the ordinary purchaser?

choices.A: The completely unwary consumer who knows nothing about the product.
choices.B: An expert who studies every label under a microscope.
choices.C: The ordinarily intelligent buyer, considering the type of product involved, who is accustomed to buy, and therefore somewhat familiar with, the goods in question.
choices.D: The manufacturer's own sales agent.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court quoted the rule that more credit should be given to the ordinary purchaser, who is not the completely unwary consumer but the ordinarily intelligent buyer considering the type of product involved, as defined in Dy Buncio v. Tan Tiao Bok: one accustomed to buy, and therefore to some extent familiar with, the goods in question. The test of fraudulent simulation is the likelihood of deception of persons somewhat acquainted with an established design and desirous of purchasing the commodity, not of a person who knows nothing about the design. A is the opposite of the test. B and D are not what the Court said.

source.caseTitle: Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc.
source.part: The ordinarily intelligent buyer is not likely to be confused
source.excerpt: Finally, in line with the foregoing discussions, more credit should be given to the "ordinary purchaser." Cast in this particular controversy, the ordinary purchaser is not the "completely unwary consumer" but is the "ordinarily intelligent buyer" considering the type of product involved.

questions.prompt: The Court of Appeals' factual findings in Taiwan Kolin Corporation, Ltd. v. Kolin Electronics Co., Inc. are normally given great respect. Why did the Supreme Court nevertheless reverse the Court of Appeals on the question of whether the goods are related?

choices.B: Because the Court of Appeals had no jurisdiction over the case.
choices.C: Because the parties agreed to waive the Court of Appeals' findings.
choices.D: Because the policy of respecting factual findings does not bind where the lower courts overlooked, misapprehended or misapplied any fact or circumstance of weight and substance, and the nature of the products materially affects the outcome.

The Court noted on a final point that the policy of according great respect, if not finality, to the factual findings of the courts below is not binding where they have overlooked, misapprehended or misapplied any fact or circumstance of weight and substance, and that here the nature of the products involved materially affects the outcome. A is wrong because the Court did recognize the general policy. B and C are not reasons the Court gave. The Court then reversed the Court of Appeals' decision and resolution and reinstated the Decision of the IPO Director General.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company has long sold a seasonal food product in a red paper bag with a picture of a partly sliced product served with fruits on the front and other products listed at the back, under its registered brand FIESTA. A competitor sells the same kind of product under a different word, PISTA, which sounds similar and means the same, and switches from its old box to a red paper bag with the same layout. Each bag carries its maker's house mark. The first company sues for unfair competition. What are the elements, and is the competitor liable even if its mark is not an infringement? Explain, based on San Miguel Pure Foods Company, Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. The competitor may be liable for unfair competition even if its mark does not infringe, because unfair competition looks at the general appearance of the goods and the intent to deceive, not only at the marks.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 168 of the Intellectual Property Code, a person who has identified in the mind of the public the goods he manufactures, whether or not a registered mark is employed, has a property right in the goodwill of those goods, and any person who employs deception or other means contrary to good faith to pass off his goods as those of one with established goodwill, or who gives his goods the general appearance of goods of another manufacturer or dealer, is guilty of unfair competition. Unfair competition is the passing off or attempting to pass off upon the public of the goods or business of one person as those of another, with the end and probable effect of deceiving the public. The essential elements are (1) confusing similarity in the general appearance of the goods and (2) intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor. The confusing similarity may result from other external factors in the packaging or presentation of the goods, and the intent to deceive may be inferred from the similarity of the appearance of the goods as offered for sale.
suggestedAnswer.application: The competitor's packaging in its entirety, and not merely its mark, is confusingly similar: both are paper bags, both are predominantly red, and both have the same layout of a partly sliced product with fruits in front and other varieties at the back. This would likely influence purchasers to believe that the goods are the first company's. Its intent to deceive and ride on the other's goodwill is shown by the switch from its own box to the same kind of bag with the same layout, and it may be inferred from the similarity. One may ask why, of the millions of designs and packaging available, it had to choose one so close to the other's. The presence of a house mark on each bag does not remove the confusing similarity of the general appearance.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The competitor is liable for unfair competition, even if it did not infringe the mark.

keyPoints: Section 168.1: goodwill is protected as property whether or not a registered mark is employed
Unfair competition is passing off one's goods as those of another, with the end and probable effect of deceiving the public
Elements: (1) confusing similarity in the general appearance of the goods; and (2) intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor
The confusing similarity may result from packaging or presentation and not only from the marks
Intent to deceive may be inferred from the similarity of the appearance of the goods; actual fraudulent intent need not be shown
Switching to the same kind of bag and the same layout showed intent to deceive

source.caseTitle: San Miguel Pure Foods Company, Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc.
source.part: G.R. No. 217788: Foodsphere is guilty of unfair competition
source.excerpt: Thus, the essential elements of an action for unfair competition are: (1) confusing similarity in the general appearance of the goods; and (2) intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor. … First of all, there exists a substantial and confusing similarity in the packaging of Foodsphere's product with that of SMPFCI, which, as the records reveal, was changed by Foodsphere from a paper box to a paper ham bag that is significantly similar to SMPFCI's paper ham bag. As duly noted by the Director General and the CA, both packages use paper ham bags as the container for the hams, both paper ham bags use the red color as the main colors, and both have the layout design appearing on the bags consisting of a partly sliced ham and fruits on the front and other ham varieties offered at the back. Thus, Foodsphere's packaging in its entirety, and not merely its "PISTA" mark thereon, renders the general appearance thereof confusingly similar with the packaging of SMPFCI's ham, that would likely influence purchasers to believe that these products are similar, if not the same, as those of SMPFCI. Second of all, Foodsphere's intent to deceive the public, to defraud its competitor, and to ride on the goodwill of SMPFCI's products is evidenced by the fact that not only did Foodsphere switch from its old box packaging to the same paper ham bag packaging as that used by SMPFCI, it also used the same layout design printed on the same.
