questions.prompt: The body of an appellate court's decision says that an award of exemplary damages "was warranted", but the dispositive portion only says that the petition is denied and that the decision of the lower agency, which had not awarded exemplary damages, is affirmed. The winning party argues that the body of the decision controls and that it is entitled to exemplary damages. Is the party right? Explain, based on San Miguel Pure Foods Company, Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. When the dispositive portion (fallo) conflicts with the body of the decision, the fallo prevails. The exception does not apply here, because the mistake is in the body and the court only meant to adopt the lower agency's award, which did not include exemplary damages.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: When there is a conflict between the fallo of a decision and the opinion of the court in its body, the fallo prevails. The rule rests on the theory that the fallo is the final order, while the body is merely a statement ordering nothing, and an order of execution is based on the disposition, not the body. There is an exception: the body prevails where the inevitable conclusion from the body is so clear as to show that there was a mistake in the dispositive portion.
suggestedAnswer.application: The exception requires a mistake in the dispositive portion. Here the mistake, if any, lay in the body. The appellate court's statements, such as that the party was "correctly ordered" to pay nominal damages, that the lower agency had no basis to award lost profits, that the award of attorney's fees "must likewise be upheld", and its disposition denying the petition and affirming the lower agency's decision, show that it meant merely to adopt the agency's award. Since the affirmed decision awarded only nominal damages and attorney's fees and no exemplary damages, the appellate court did not intend to award them, and so what controls is the fallo.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The party is not entitled to exemplary damages on that ground; the dispositive portion controls.

This rule rests on the theory that the fallo is the final order, while the opinion in the body is merely a statement ordering nothing. Thus, an order of execution is based on the disposition, not on the body, of the Decision. Contrary to SMPFCI's assertion, moreover, the Court finds inapplicable the exception to the foregoing rule which states that the body of the decision will prevail in instances where the inevitable conclusion from the body of the decision is so clear as to show that there was a mistake in the dispositive portion. … It can, therefore, be derived, from the wording of the CA Decision, that it merely intended to adopt the resolution of the Director General on the award of damages. questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company wins an unfair competition case but fails to present sufficient evidence of its claimed lost income. It then asks for exemplary damages, arguing that the competitor acted deceptively. May exemplary damages be awarded? Explain the requisites, based on San Miguel Pure Foods Company, Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Exemplary damages cannot be recovered as a matter of right. The claimant must first establish its right to moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages, and the company failed to prove its claimed lost income.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Article 2233 of the Civil Code, exemplary damages cannot be recovered as a matter of right, and the court decides whether they should be adjudicated. Under Article 2234, while the amount need not be proven, the plaintiff must show that he is entitled to moral, temperate or compensatory damages before the court may consider whether exemplary damages should be awarded. The requisites are: (1) they may be imposed, by way of example, only in addition, among others, to compensatory damages, only after the claimant's right to them has been established; (2) the claimant must first establish his right to moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages; and (3) the act must be accompanied by bad faith or done in a wanton, fraudulent, oppressive or malevolent manner.
suggestedAnswer.application: The second requisite is missing. The company claimed foregone income, but it did not present sufficient evidence of its lost income or sales, nor of its profit, and so it did not prove its right to compensatory damages, nor to moral or temperate damages. Without that, exemplary damages cannot be considered, even though the competitor's conduct may have been deceptive. It was only entitled to the nominal damages and attorney's fees that were awarded.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Exemplary damages are not awarded, because the right to moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages was not established.

keyPoints: Exemplary damages cannot be recovered as a matter of right (Article 2233)
The claimant must show that it is entitled to moral, temperate or compensatory damages before exemplary damages are considered (Article 2234)

Three requisites: addition to compensatory damages after the right is established; prior proof of moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages; bad faith or wanton, fraudulent, oppressive or malevolent act
Failure to prove foregone income or sales means that the right to compensatory damages was not established
Nominal damages and attorney's fees were awarded instead

source.excerpt: Article 2233 of the Civil Code provides that exemplary damages cannot be recovered as a matter of right; the court will decide whether or not they should be adjudicated while Article 2234 thereof provides that while the amount of the exemplary damages need not be proven, the plaintiff must show that he is entitled to moral, temperate or compensatory damages before the court may consider the question of whether or not exemplary damages should be awarded. … (1) they may be imposed, by way of example, only in addition, among others, to compensatory damages, only after the claimant's right to them has been established, and cannot be recovered as a matter of right, their determination depending upon the amount of compensatory damages that may be awarded to the claimant; (2) the claimant must first establish his right to moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages; and (3) the act must be accompanied by bad faith or done in a wanton, fraudulent, oppressive or malevolent manner. … But as the Director General aptly found, SMPFCI neither adduced sufficient evidence to prove its claim of foregone income or sales nor presented evidence to show the profit or sales.

questions.prompt: In San Miguel Pure Foods Company, Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc., what is the "true test" of unfair competition?

choices.A: Whether the defendant's acts have the intent of deceiving or are calculated to deceive the ordinary buyer making his purchases under the ordinary conditions of the particular trade to which the controversy relates.
choices.B: Whether the defendant's goods are cheaper than the plaintiff's goods.
choices.C: Whether the plaintiff's mark is registered in the Philippines.
choices.D: Whether the defendant's mark is spelled exactly like the plaintiff's.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court explained that unfair competition consists of the passing off, or attempting to pass off, of the goods or business of one person as those of another with the end and probable effect of deceiving the public. Passing off takes place where the defendant, by imitative devices on the general appearance of the goods, misleads prospective purchasers into buying his merchandise under the impression that they are buying that of his competitor. The true test is whether the defendant's acts have the intent of deceiving, or are calculated to deceive, the ordinary buyer making purchases under the ordinary conditions of the particular trade. B, C and D are not the test: registration is not needed, and the confusing similarity may or may not result from similarity in the marks.

It added that factual findings of administrative agencies are generally accorded respect and even finality if supported by substantial evidence, since these agencies are presumed to have knowledge and expertise in matters under their jurisdiction, more so when the findings are affirmed by the Court of Appeals. A and C are the opposite of the Court's approach. D is wrong because the Court itself affirmed the finding.

questions.prompt: A producer holds a copyright certificate for a television game show. Another network airs a show with the same arrangement: contestants of one gender who cannot see the other group ask questions, and a match is made from the answers. The producer files a complaint for copyright infringement, arguing that its show's format and mechanics are copyrightable and were copied. Is the format of the show protected by copyright? Explain, based on Joaquin, Jr. v. Drilon.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The format or mechanics of a television show is not among the works that the copyright law protects. Copyright is purely statutory and extends only to the classes of works that the statute lists, and it does not cover ideas, concepts or methods.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Copyright in the strict sense is purely a statutory right: a new or independent right granted by statute, not a pre-existing right regulated by it, so the rights are only those the statute confers, and may be obtained only for the subjects, by the persons and on the terms the statute specifies. A copyright may be obtained only for a work falling within the statutory enumeration. Section 2 of P.D. No. 49 enumerates the classes of protected works (such as books, musical compositions, works of art, cinematographic works and computer programs), substantially the same as Section 172 of the Intellectual Property Code. It refers to finished works and not to concepts. The copyright does not extend to an idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept or principle, however described or embodied in a work (see Section 175 of the Code).
suggestedAnswer.application: The format of a show, such as its arrangement and the mechanics of how matches are made, is not included in the list of protected works. The producer's copyright covers the show as a work, such as the audio-visual recordings of its episodes, but not the general concept or format that others may use. A point-by-point comparison showing that the two formats are the same therefore does not show infringement of a copyrightable work, since the format itself is not protected.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The format of the show is not copyrightable, and copying it is not copyright infringement.

The format or mechanics of a television show is not in the list of protected works in Section 2 of P.D. No. 49 (substantially the same as Section 172 of the IP Code)
The enumeration refers to finished works and not to concepts
Copyright does not extend to an idea, procedure, system, method of operation, concept or principle (Section 175 of the IP Code)
What is protected is the work itself, such as the audio-visual recording of each episode

No. 49, otherwise known as the DECREE ON INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY, enumerates the classes of work entitled to copyright protection, to wit: … This provision is substantially the same as §172 of the INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY CODE OF PHILIPPINES (R.A. No. 8293). The format or mechanics of a television show is not included in the list of protected works in §2 of P.D. No. 49. For this reason, the protection afforded by the law cannot be extended to cover them. … The copyright does not extend to the general concept or format of its dating game show.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A producer complains that another company copied its television show. During the preliminary investigation, it submits only written descriptions of the formats of the two shows and a point-by-point comparison, without the master videotape of its copyrighted show. The prosecutor finds probable cause, but the Secretary of Justice reverses, saying the master tape was needed. The producer says that the tape had never been raised as an issue, and that the description is enough. Who is right? Explain, based on Joaquin, Jr. v. Drilon.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Secretary of Justice is right. A written description of the format is insufficient, and the master videotape was indispensable to determining probable cause, because a television show includes more than words can describe. The Secretary may also consider an error that the parties did not raise.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In reviewing prosecutors' resolutions, the Secretary of Justice is not precluded from considering errors, although unassigned, to determine whether there is probable cause; he must make his own finding and is not confined to the issues raised during the preliminary investigation. The essence of copyright infringement is the similarity or at least substantial similarity of the purported pirated work to the copyrighted work, so the copyrighted work must be presented for comparison, although the requirement of the master tape is only a guidepost, not a sweeping and inflexible requirement in all copyright infringement cases (Columbia Pictures v. Court of Appeals, qualifying 20th Century Fox v. Court of Appeals).
suggestedAnswer.application: The producer's copyright covers the audio-visual recordings of its episodes and not the general concept or format of its show. By the very nature of what is protected, the investigating prosecutor needed to compare the videotapes of the two shows. A television show involves a whole spectrum of visuals and effects, video and audio, so that no similarity or dissimilarity can be found by merely describing the general format of both shows. Since the producer presented only descriptions of formats, which are not protected, probable cause was not shown, and the Secretary was entitled to consider this point even if the respondents never raised it.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The master videotape was needed, and the Secretary of Justice did not gravely abuse his discretion in reversing the finding of probable cause.

The essence of copyright infringement is similarity or substantial similarity to the copyrighted work
The copyright covers the audio-visual recordings of each episode, not the general concept or format
A television show includes more than words can describe, so a mere description of the format is insufficient
The master tape requirement is a guidepost where there is doubt about the nexus, not an inflexible rule (Columbia Pictures)

Accordingly, by the very nature of the subject of petitioner BJPI's copyright, the investigating prosecutor should have the opportunity to compare the videotapes of the two shows. Mere description by words of the general format of the two dating game shows is insufficient; the presentation of the master videotape in evidence was indispensable to the determination of the existence of probable cause. suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Whether the format of a show is entitled to copyright protection is a legal question for the court to decide, but this does not stop the Secretary of Justice from making a preliminary determination of it in deciding whether there is probable cause.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A preliminary investigation falls under the authority of the state prosecutor, who has the power to direct and control criminal actions, subject to the control of the Secretary of Justice. In reviewing prosecutors' resolutions, the Secretary is not precluded from considering errors, although unassigned, to determine whether there is probable cause, and he must make his own finding. His findings are not subject to review unless shown to have been made with grave abuse. The question of whether a format is entitled to copyright protection is a legal question for the court, but the Secretary may make a preliminary determination of it when resolving whether there is probable cause to file the case in court.
suggestedAnswer.application: The Secretary did not decide the copyright question with finality; he made a preliminary determination, as part of resolving whether probable cause existed. In doing so he did not commit any grave error: the format of a show is not within the statutory list of works protected by copyright. Since his finding was not made with grave abuse, it is not subject to review by certiorari.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The complainant is not correct. The Secretary of Justice acted within his authority in preliminarily determining that the format was not copyrightable.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court held that BJPI's copyright covers audio-visual recordings of each episode of Rhoda and Me, as falling within the class of works mentioned in Section 2(M) of P.D. No. 49: cinematographic works and works produced by a process analogous to cinematography or any process for making audio-visual recordings. The copyright does not extend to the general concept or format of its dating game show. A and C are what the Court said the copyright does not cover. D is not what the decision says is protected.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A manufacturer registers its engineering drawings of a lighted advertising box with the copyright office, as a work under the class of "prints, pictorial illustrations, advertising copies, labels, tags and box wraps", and titles the certificate "Advertising Display Units". A store has similar boxes made by a contractor and leases them to advertisers. The manufacturer sues for copyright infringement, claiming that its copyright extends to the boxes themselves. Will the suit prosper? Explain, based on Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The copyright covers only the technical drawings, not the boxes. Making boxes similar to those illustrated in the drawings is not copying the drawings, so there is no copyright infringement.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Copyright in the strict sense is purely statutory. The rights are limited to what the statute confers, and may be obtained only for the subjects, by the persons and on the terms the statute specifies, so copyright can cover only the works falling within the statutory enumeration or description. Section 2 of P.D. No. 49 listed the protected works, and class (O) covered prints, pictorial illustrations, advertising copies, labels, tags and box wraps. What the law does not include, it excludes, and a certificate cannot be stretched by the title it is given.
suggestedAnswer.application: The manufacturer secured its copyright as a class (O) work, so its protection extended only to the technical drawings, which fall within "pictorial illustrations", and not to the light box, which is not in that category and is not a literary or artistic piece. Entitling the certificate "Advertising Display Units" does not supply the missing statutory authority. If the store had reprinted the drawings for sale, it would have infringed the copyright. But what it did was have units made that are similar or identical to the box illustrated in the drawings, and that does not infringe the copyright in the drawings.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The suit fails. The copyright in the drawings does not extend to the light box itself.

keyPoints: Copyright is purely statutory and covers only works within the statutory enumeration
The certificate was for a class (O) work: prints, pictorial illustrations, advertising copies, labels, tags and box wraps
The copyright extended only to the technical drawings and not to the light box
What the law does not include, it excludes, and the title of the certificate cannot expand it
Reprinting the drawings would infringe, but making similar boxes does not infringe the copyright in the drawings

source.caseTitle: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Incorporated v. Shoemart, Incorporated and North Edsa Marketing, Incorporated
source.part: On the issue of copyright infringement
source.excerpt: Copyright, in the strict sense of the term, is purely a statutory right. Being a mere statutory grant, the rights are limited to what the statute confers. It may be obtained and enjoyed only with respect to the subjects and by the persons, and on terms and conditions specified in the statute. Accordingly, it can cover only the works falling within the statutory enumeration or description. … P & D secured its copyright under the classification class "O" work. This being so, petitioner’s copyright protection extended only to the technical drawings and not to the light box itself because the latter was not at all in the category of "prints, pictorial illustrations, advertising copies, labels, tags and box wraps." … What the law does not include, it excludes, and for the good reason: the light box was not a literary or artistic piece which could be copyrighted under the copyright law. … In fine, if SMI and NEMI reprinted P & D’s technical drawings for sale to the public without license from P & D, then no doubt they would have been guilty of copyright infringement. But this was not the case.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: An inventor has a copyright certificate for the drawings of a new useful device. It never applied for a patent on the device. A competitor manufactures and sells the same device. The inventor argues that, because the copyright lasts for many years and the device is its invention, the competitor must stop. Is the inventor right? Explain the difference between copyright and patent protection, based on Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Without a patent, the inventor cannot stop others from making or selling the device. A copyright over the drawings protects the drawings, not the invention, and the exclusivity over an invention can be obtained only through a patent after examination.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Trademark, copyright and patent are different intellectual property rights that cannot be interchanged. There can be no infringement of a patent until a patent has been issued, since the right to the invention arises only from the grant of the patent. An inventor has no common law right to a monopoly of his invention: if he voluntarily discloses it, the world is free to copy and use it with impunity. To effectively preclude others from copying and profiting from the invention, a patent is a primordial requirement: no patent, no protection. A patent is issued only after an exhaustive examination by the patent office, while a copyright arises from the moment of creation and the certificate is issued on a sworn ex parte claim, without such scrutiny. In Baker v. Selden, only the expression of an idea is protected by copyright, not the idea or art described, which is the province of letters patent.
suggestedAnswer.application: The inventor never secured a patent, so it acquired no patent rights and could not legally prevent anyone from manufacturing or commercially using the device. By submitting its drawings to the copyright office, it disclosed the device to the public without the protection of a patent. A copyright over the drawings does not give the exclusive right to make and sell the device drawn. If it were otherwise, the inventor would obtain through the simplified copyright procedure, and for a longer period, an exclusivity that it would have had to earn by defending patentability before the patent office, and the Court said that this could not have been the intention of the law.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The inventor is not right. Without a patent, the competitor may freely make and sell the device.

keyPoints: Trademark, copyright and patent are distinct rights that cannot be used interchangeably
No patent, no protection: there can be no patent infringement until a patent is issued
An inventor who discloses the invention without a patent leaves the world free to copy it
Patents are issued only after exhaustive examination; copyright arises from creation on a sworn ex parte claim without scrutiny
Copyright protects the expression and not the idea or the art described (Baker v. Selden)
Copyright would not be allowed to give a longer exclusivity than a patent without the examination

source.caseTitle: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Incorporated v. Shoemart, Incorporated and North Edsa Marketing, Incorporated
source.part: On the issue of patent infringement
source.excerpt: For some reason or another, petitioner never secured a patent for the light boxes. It therefore acquired no patent rights which could have protected its invention, if in fact it really was. And because it had no patent, petitioner could not legally prevent anyone from manufacturing or commercially using the contraption. … To be able to effectively and legally preclude others from copying and profiting from the invention, a patent is a primordial requirement. No patent, no protection. … Therefore, not having gone through the arduous examination for patents, the petitioner cannot exclude others from the manufacture, sale or commercial use of the light boxes on the sole basis of its copyright certificate over the technical drawings. Stated otherwise, what petitioner seeks is exclusivity without any opportunity for the patent office (IPO) to scrutinize the light box’s eligibility as a patentable invention. The irony here is that, had petitioner secured a patent instead, its exclusivity would have been for 17 years only. But through the simplified procedure of copyright-registration with the National Library — without undergoing the rigor of defending the patentability of its invention before the IPO and the public — the petitioner would be protected for 50 years. This situation could not have been the intention of the law.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company registers the phrase "Poster Ads" as a trademark, but its certificate lists only stationeries such as letterheads and envelopes, which it does not actually sell. Its real business is lighted advertising boxes, and "Poster Ads" is a contraction of "poster advertising". When a competitor uses "Poster Ads" for its advertising boxes, the company sues for trademark infringement and unfair competition. Will either claim prosper? Explain, based on Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The registration protects the mark only for the goods specified in the certificate, which are not the advertising boxes, so there is no trademark infringement. And as a generic term with no secondary meaning, the phrase is not protected against unfair competition either.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A certificate of registration gives the exclusive right to use the mark only for the goods specified in the certificate, subject to its conditions and limitations; one who has adopted a mark on his goods does not prevent others from adopting the same mark for products of a different description (Faberge, applying Section 20 of the old Trademark Law). Registration is an essential element of trademark infringement. Unfair competition may exist even without registration, but a name or phrase that is incapable of appropriation as a trademark may be protected against unfair competition only if, by long and exclusive use, it has become associated with the business or product in the mind of the purchasing public, that is, if it has acquired secondary meaning.
suggestedAnswer.application: The company's certificate specified only stationeries, which it did not sell, and not the lighted advertising boxes, so even if "Poster Ads" could qualify as a trademark, the company's failure to register it for use on the advertising boxes meant that there could be no trademark infringement. As for unfair competition, "Poster Ads" is a generic contraction of poster advertising, the very field of the company's business, and the company's own expert admitted that the name was too generic to be identified with any company. That admission shows that the public does not associate the name with the company, which rules out secondary meaning and any protection against unfair competition.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Neither claim prospers. There is no infringement of the registered mark and no unfair competition.

keyPoints: The exclusive right under a registration is limited to the goods specified in the certificate
Registration is an essential element of trademark infringement
Use of the same mark by others on goods of a different description is not prevented by the registrant's mark
A generic term such as the contraction of "poster advertising" cannot be appropriated as a trademark
Without secondary meaning (long and exclusive use that makes the public associate the phrase with one business), there is no protection against unfair competition
The admission of the company's own expert that the name was too generic prevented secondary meaning

source.caseTitle: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Incorporated v. Shoemart, Incorporated and North Edsa Marketing, Incorporated
source.part: On the issues of trademark infringement and unfair competition
source.excerpt: This issue concerns the use by respondents of the mark "Poster Ads" which petitioner’s president said was a contraction of "poster advertising." P & D was able to secure a trademark certificate for it, but one where the goods specified were "stationeries such as letterheads, envelopes, calling cards and newsletters." Petitioner admitted it did not commercially engage in or market these goods. … One who has adopted and used a trademark on his goods does not prevent the adoption and use of the same trademark by others for products which are of a different description. … By the nature of things, there can be no unfair competition under the law on copyrights although it is applicable to disputes over the use of trademarks. Even a name or phrase incapable of appropriation as a trademark or tradename may, by long and exclusive use by a business (such that the name or phrase becomes associated with the business or product in the mind of the purchasing public), be entitled to protection against unfair competition. … This fact also prevented the application of the doctrine of secondary meaning. "Poster Ads" was generic and incapable of being used as a trademark because it was used in the field of poster advertising, the very business engaged in by petitioner.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company confuses its trademark, copyright and patent. According to Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc. (quoting Kho v. Court of Appeals), which statement about these three rights is correct?

choices.A: They are the same right under different names and may be used interchangeably.
choices.B: A copyright covers any invention that is new and useful.
choices.C: They are different intellectual property rights that cannot be interchanged: a trademark distinguishes goods or services, a copyright is confined to literary and artistic works, and a patent covers new, inventive and industrially applicable technical solutions.
choices.D: A trademark protects the technical features of a product.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court, quoting Kho v. Court of Appeals, said that trademark, copyright and patents are different intellectual property rights that cannot be interchanged. A trademark is any visible sign capable of distinguishing the goods or services of an enterprise, and a trade name is the name identifying an enterprise. The scope of a copyright is confined to literary and artistic works which are original intellectual creations in the literary and artistic domain, protected from the moment of creation. Patentable inventions are technical solutions of a problem in any field of human activity which are new, involve an inventive step and are industrially applicable. A is the opposite of the rule. B and D mix up the rights, which is exactly the confusion that the Court corrected in this case.

source.caseTitle: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Incorporated v. Shoemart, Incorporated and North Edsa Marketing, Incorporated
source.part: On the issue of copyright infringement (Kho v. Court of Appeals)
source.excerpt: In the leading case of Kho vs. Court of Appeals, we ruled that these three legal rights are completely distinct and separate from one another, and the protection afforded by one cannot be used interchangeably to cover items or works that exclusively pertain to the others: Trademark, copyright and patents are different intellectual property rights that cannot be interchanged with one another. A trademark is any visible sign capable of distinguishing the goods (trademark) or services (service mark) of an enterprise and shall include a stamped or marked container of goods. In relation thereto, a trade name means the name or designation identifying or distinguishing an enterprise. Meanwhile, the scope of a copyright is confined to literary and artistic works which are original intellectual creations in the literary and artistic domain protected from the moment of their creation. Patentable inventions, on the other hand, refer to any technical solution of a problem in any field of human activity which is new, involves an inventive step and is industrially applicable.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., how does the way in which a copyright is obtained differ from the way in which a patent is obtained?

choices.A: A copyright requires an exhaustive examination, while a patent arises automatically.
choices.B: Both are obtained only after a published notice and opposition.
choices.C: Neither requires any registration.
choices.D: A patent is issued only after an exhaustive examination by the patent office, while a copyright is conferred from the moment of creation and the certificate is issued on registration of a sworn ex parte claim of creation, without such scrutiny or published notice.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court explained that it is only after an exhaustive examination by the patent office that a patent is issued, because the prerequisites for a patent are strictly observed. There is no such scrutiny for copyrights, nor any notice published before the grant that a person is claiming the creation of a work: the law confers the copyright from the moment of creation, and the certificate is issued upon registration with the National Library of a sworn ex parte claim of creation. A reverses the two. B is wrong because copyright has no published notice. C is wrong because a patent must be applied for and issued. Watch for: this describes the copyright law then in force (P.D. No. 49) as applied in the decision; check the current law on copyright.

source.caseTitle: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Incorporated v. Shoemart, Incorporated and North Edsa Marketing, Incorporated
source.part: On the issue of patent infringement (the difference in examination)
source.excerpt: It is only after an exhaustive examination by the patent office that a patent is issued. … There is no such scrutiny in the case of copyrights nor any notice published before its grant to the effect that a person is claiming the creation of a work. The law confers the copyright from the moment of creation and the copyright certificate is issued upon registration with the National Library of a sworn ex-parte claim of creation.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc. (quoting Creser Precision Systems), what is the situation of an inventor who discloses his invention to the public without a patent?

choices.A: The world is free to copy and use the invention with impunity, because the right to exclude others arises only from the grant of a patent.
choices.B: He keeps a common law monopoly over the invention.
choices.C: He may exclude others through the doctrine of equivalents.
choices.D: He may exclude others for as long as he keeps the invention in use.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court quoted that there can be no infringement of a patent until a patent has been issued, since whatever right one has to the invention arises alone from the grant of the patent. An inventor has no common law right to a monopoly of his invention: he has the right to make, use and vend it, but if he voluntarily discloses it, such as by offering it for sale, the world is free to copy and use it with impunity. A patent gives the inventor the right to exclude all others. B is the opposite of the quoted rule. C is wrong because equivalents is a test of infringement of an existing patent. D has no basis in the decision.

source.caseTitle: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Incorporated v. Shoemart, Incorporated and North Edsa Marketing, Incorporated
source.part: On the issue of patent infringement (Creser Precision Systems)
source.excerpt: In Creser Precision Systems, Inc. vs. Court of Appeals, we held that "there can be no infringement of a patent until a patent has been issued, since whatever right one has to the invention covered by the patent arises alone from the grant of patent. x x x (A)n inventor has no common law right to a monopoly of his invention. He has the right to make use of and vend his invention, but if he voluntarily discloses it, such as by offering it for sale, the world is free to copy and use it with impunity. A patent, however, gives the inventor the right to exclude all others.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company has a trademark certificate that lists certain goods but never registered the mark for the goods that it actually sells. A competitor uses the same words on those goods. According to Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., what is the consequence for a claim of trademark infringement?

choices.A: The claim prospers, because any registered mark is protected for all goods.
choices.B: There can be no trademark infringement, because registration for the specific use on those goods was an essential element and it was missing.
choices.C: The claim prospers if the competitor's goods are cheaper.
choices.D: The claim prospers if the competitor is a large company.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court said that, assuming that "Poster Ads" could validly qualify as a trademark, the failure of P & D to secure a trademark registration for specific use on the light boxes meant that there could not have been any trademark infringement, since registration was an essential element of it. It invoked Faberge and Section 20 of the old Trademark Law: the certificate confers the exclusive right to use the symbol only for the goods specified in it, and the registrant did not even sell the goods named in its certificate. A is the opposite of the rule. C and D are not factors. Watch for: this is the rule under the old Trademark Law applied in the decision; check the current law for registrations under the Intellectual Property Code.

source.part: On the issue of trademark infringement
source.excerpt: Assuming arguendo that "Poster Ads" could validly qualify as a trademark, the failure of P & D to secure a trademark registration for specific use on the light boxes meant that there could not have been any trademark infringement since registration was an essential element thereof.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc. (discussing Baker v. Selden), what does a copyright over a book that describes an art or system protect?

choices.A: The exclusive right to practice the art or system described in the book.
choices.B: The exclusive right to make and sell everything illustrated in the book.
choices.C: Every idea contained in the book.
choices.D: Only the expression, that is, the book itself as a work; the art it describes can be secured, if at all, only by a patent.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court recalled Baker v. Selden: only the expression of an idea is protected by copyright, not the idea itself. A copyright on a book explaining an art gives the exclusive right to print and publish the book, but no one is prevented from practicing and using the art that the book describes; the object of the book is explanation and the object of the art is use. The former may be secured by copyright, and the latter can only be secured, if it can be secured at all, by letters patent. A, B and C claim exactly the exclusive right to the art or the idea that the rule denies.

source.caseTitle: Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Incorporated v. Shoemart, Incorporated and North Edsa Marketing, Incorporated
source.part: On the issue of patent infringement (Baker v. Selden)
source.excerpt: In the oft-cited case of Baker vs. Selden, the United States Supreme Court held that only the expression of an idea is protected by copyright, not the idea itself. … The description of the art in a book, though entitled to the benefit of copyright, lays no foundation for an exclusive claim to the art itself. The object of the one is explanation; the object of the other is use. The former may be secured by copyright. The latter can only be secured, if it can be secured at all, by letters patent.
